Don’t distract Oyebanji with 2030 politics, Tinubu warns
items.description: Governor pledges to serve with greater humility By Rotimi Ojomoyela ADO-EKITI — President Bola Tinubu has cautioned politicians in Ekiti State against declaring interest in the 2030 governorship election while Governor Biodun Oyebanji is beginning his second term, warning that premature politicking could distract the administration and undermine governance. Tinubu gave the warning on Sunday at a thanksgiving service marking Oyebanji’s second-term inauguration, where the governor pledged to intensify efforts to tackle poverty and unemployment, promote industrialisation and drive economic growth. Oyebanji and his deputy, Chief Monisade Afuye, were inaugurated for a second term on Friday at the Ekitiparapo Pavilion in Ado-Ekiti, at a ceremony attended by the President. Speaking at the thanksgiving service held at the Cathedral Church of Emmanuel, Okesa, Ado-Ekiti, Tinubu, who was represented by Senate Leader, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, urged the political class to place the collective interest of the state above personal ambition. He commended Oyebanji for completing his first term and urged him to sustain his inclusive approach to governance and respect for all citizens. “To the political class, let us show love to this administration. Let us show love to Ekiti. Loyalty to Governor Oyebanji is loyalty to Ekiti. It is when we are loyal that we won’t distract him or start declaring to occupy his seat so early,” Tinubu said. He added: “Whoever says he wants to become the governor in the next three years is an enemy of progress. Let us bear in mind that the moment you declare interest in governorship, there will be distraction. “Don’t let us see politics as the only industry in Ekiti. Let us think of other things and look at the larger picture and the interest of Ekiti.” The President urged Oyebanji to remain focused, humble and accessible throughout his second term. “I appeal to you, continue to be whom you are. Let no one, not the traditional rulers, not the former governors, not the political class, not the civil servants, not the women or youth groups change whom you are,” he said. Tinubu described Oyebanji’s return for a second term as an opportunity to consolidate on his achievements, noting that continuity in governance should translate into better performance. “You are not the first governor to run for a second term, but to the glory of God, you were the first to hand over to yourself. Others fought hard to come back. This was a grace,” he said. “Whoever breaks the jinx of second term after you will have you as a reference point. There is power in continuity, so you must work hard to ensure continuity in this state. God will help you to perform better.” In his remarks, Oyebanji thanked the people of Ekiti for their support and promised that his second term would deliver greater benefits, with emphasis on industrialisation and shared prosperity. “Let me assure you that my second term will be better than the first term with emphasis on industrialisation and prosperity for our people. In our first, we had put infrastructures in place to attract investors to this state. With industrialisation, employment will be here and everyone will prosper,” the governor said. He, however, stressed that attracting industries would require cooperation between the government, traditional rulers and communities, particularly on land acquisition for investors. “But government alone can’t do it, so we are partnering with our traditional rulers on the issue of land. Investors won’t come when people are not ready to release lands and if there is no cooperation from the people, there will be problem. There are sacrifices we have to make to bring industries here,” he said. The governor acknowledged the responsibility arising from the support he received in the last election, pledging to serve the people with humility and remain accessible. “I know I am confronted with the burden of 87.7% of total votes cast you gave me in the last election. I know that the only way I can go is for me to serve Ekiti in the way that glorifies God. “I promise before God and man today that I will serve you with humility, listen to you and connect with you,” he said. Oyebanji added that he hoped to leave office with a record that would earn him the respect of the people and his predecessors. “It is my desire that after my exit, I should be able to walk tall like my predecessors are doing,” he said. In his homily, the Bishop of Ekiti Diocese, Anglican Communion, Rt. Rev. Andrew Olusola Ajayi, urged the governor to regard his position as a trust to be exercised in the interest of the people. The cleric said Oyebanji’s second term should be devoted to serving God and humanity, warning that public office carried a responsibility for which he would ultimately be accountable. “Do you know what God wants from you in this second term, it is for you to serve Him and humanity. You are not the owner of Ekiti State, but a steward,” Ajayi said. He urged the governor to maintain his integrity and sustain the qualities that had earned him public trust. “People are talking good things about you. Please, continue in this goodness. You should also maintain your integrity. You are a man of integrity, you must know this,” he said. The First Lady, Prof. Olayemi Oyebanji, led choristers in a special rendition during the service. Dignitaries at the event included former governors Niyi Adebayo, Ayodele Fayose and Segun Oni; former Governor Kayode Fayemi, represented by his wife, Erelu Bisi Fayemi; Senators Yemi Adaramodu and Cyril Fasuyi; and members of the House of Representatives, Femi Bamisile, Sola Fatoba and Biodun Omoleye. Traditional rulers, religious leaders, labour leaders, traders and civil servants were also present. The post Don’t distract Oyebanji with 2030 politics, Tinubu warns appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.description: Le lundi 12 octobre 2026, à 16 heures, une délégation de Publicitaires Associés (PA) a été reçue en audience par le Camarade Ministre de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, Monsieur Gilbert Pingdwendé OUÉDRAOGO, à son cabinet. Conduite par son Président, le Camarade Difaby SOMBIÉ, cette délégation est venue présenter officiellement au Ministre les membres du nouveau Bureau Exécutif National (BEN), mandat 2026-2029, ainsi que les grandes orientations et ambitions qui guideront son action au cours des trois prochaines années. À cette occasion, le Président des PA a réaffirmé la volonté du nouveau bureau de poursuivre les efforts engagés pour la structuration, la professionnalisation, la défense des intérêts et la valorisation du secteur de la publicité au Burkina Faso. En retour, le Camarade Ministre a salué cette démarche, félicité les membres du nouveau bureau et les a encouragés à poursuivre avec détermination leur engagement en faveur du développement du secteur publicitaire. Il les a notamment exhortés à continuer de se battre pour relever les défis auxquels fait face la profession. Le Ministre a également formulé ses vœux de plein succès au nouveau Bureau Exécutif National pour son mandat 2026-2029. Publicitaires Associés exprime sa profonde gratitude au Camarade Ministre pour sa disponibilité, son écoute attentive et ses encouragements. Cette audience marque une étape importante dans la dynamique de dialogue institutionnel et de collaboration entre les PA et leur ministère de tutelle. Ensemble, œuvrons pour un secteur publicitaire plus structuré, professionnel et dynamique au Burkina Faso ! items.description: Una segunda persona ha fallecido en la localidad valenciana de Oliva tras el paso de la dana Adam , según ha informado un portavoz del Consorcio Provincial de Bomberos de València y han confirmado fuentes gubernamentales. El cadáver de un hombre ha sido hallado en un cámping de la localidad y, según las primeras informaciones, ha fallecido de un infarto. Esta cuarta víctima mortal se suma a los fallecimientos registrados en Barcelona el sábado; en Sagunto el domingo y el de otra persona también en Oliva, este lunes. La fase más adversa de la dana Adam ha azotado con violencia la Comunidad Valenciana durante la madrugada, con lluvias torrenciales de hasta 700 litros por metro cuadrado en algunas zonas, que han dejado incomunicadas varias localidades en la zona costera desde el sur de Gandia hasta Oliva por las inundaciones. Los servicios de emergencia están efectuando rescates en lancha y helicóptero y, aunque a las 10.00 ha bajado el nivel del aviso meteorológico de rojo a amarillo o naranja, las autoridades instan a la población a quedarse en casa. La Generalitat ha aprobado una orden de confinamiento para 145 municipios del sur de Valencia y el norte de Alicante que afecta a cerca de 900.000 personas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: 'We never gave up': Naqvi highlights Pakistan's peace efforts in US-Iran war at Qatar forum
items.description: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday highlighted Pakistan’s mediation efforts between the United States and Iran, affirming that Islamabad “never gave up”. He made the remarks while addressing the 8th Global Security Forum being held in Qatar’s capital, Doha. Convened under the title “The Future of Alliances“, the forum brings together high-ranking officials and dignitaries from over 100 nations, according to Qatar News Agency . “The last few months have been very difficult for our region. The conflict involving Iran and the United States created serious risks not only for the Middle East, but for the entire world,” Naqvi noted. He added that at such a critical time, Pakistan chose the path of peace and made “every possible effort to reduce tensions”. Naqvi, who has been involved in Islamabad’s peace efforts and has made several trips to Iran since the war began, said, “There were moments when the situation was extremely tense, but we never gave up.” He particularly highlighted the “remarkable role” of Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir in Pakistan’s efforts to reduce tensions. CDF Munir, accompanied by Naqvi, had visited Iran in August “as part of Pakistan’s efforts to promote regional peace and stability”. The interior minister last made a visit to Iran in September , with Tehran describing the trip as part of bilateral engagements. Speaking at the Doha forum, Naqvi recalled the June 18 signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Iran and the US. The 14-point MoU , which Pakistan signed as a mediator, provided a framework for ending the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb 28. The interior minister recalled that the MoU was followed by the Lake Lucerne Summit in Switzerland, organised by mediators Pakistan and Qatar. “There, I saw something I will never forget,” he said, adding that Qatar’s Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani and CDF Munir worked for “more than 16 hours without a single break”. “No cameras, no announcements; only two men who refused to let the talks fail,” Naqvi remarked, emphasising that the only aim of the two mediating countries was to “stop further conflict”. More to follow

items.title: 48 of Ghana’s 288 forest reserves affected by galamsey – Mahama
items.description: President John Mahama has disclosed that illegal mining affected 48 of Ghana’s 288 forest reserves, saying the affected reserves have since been recovered and are undergoing reclamation. Speaking at the Mining in Motion conference on Monday, October 19, the President said heavily armed illegal miners had occupied the affected reserves, leading to their designation as red zones for enforcement officers. He said the reserves had recently been recovered, allowing reclamation work to proceed. “We have 288 forest reserves, and of these forest reserves, 48 of them had been penetrated by illegal miners,” he said at the conference in Accra. “And of the 48, 9 were declared red zones, which means the forest guards could not enter those reserves because the illegal miners were fully armed,” he added. “I am happy to note that of those 9 red zones, we have cleared all of them of illegal miners, and are currently preparing those forest reserves for reclamation,” Mr John Mahama noted. President Mahama commended those involved in the fight against illegal mining, acknowledging their efforts in reclaiming the reserves from the miners.

items.title: Immobilier : La flambée des coûts de construction met le logement économique sous pression
items.description: La hausse des prix des matériaux de construction, l’augmentation des charges énergétiques et salariales ainsi que la lenteur des procédures administratives fragilisent les promoteurs immobiliers au Maroc. Dans un marché où le pouvoir d’achat des ménages limite les marges de manœuvre sur les prix de vente, la production de logements économiques devient de plus en plus difficile, alertent des professionnels interrogés par Hespress . Le secteur de la promotion immobilière au Maroc est confronté à une hausse « brutale » des coûts des intrants, des matériaux et des moyens de production, sur fond de pressions liées à l’énergie, aux salaires et aux démarches administratives. Cette situation place les promoteurs devant un dilemme : absorber l’augmentation de leurs charges ou relever leurs prix dans un contexte où les ménages disposent d’une capacité limitée à supporter de nouvelles dépenses. Selon une source professionnelle responsable au sein de la Fédération nationale des promoteurs immobiliers, interrogée par Hespress , la faiblesse du pouvoir d’achat constitue en effet un frein à la répercussion de ces surcoûts sur les prix de vente finaux. Des matériaux de construction plus chers de 25 à 30 % Le renchérissement touche une large gamme de matériaux, notamment le sable, le fer, le ciment, le béton, le verre, le marbre et la brique. Leurs prix ont globalement augmenté de 25 % à 30 %, selon cette même source, qui suit de près l’évolution du marché immobilier national. Cette progression s’explique notamment par la hausse des coûts énergétiques. Le prix du gasoil a dépassé les 16 dirhams le litre, atteignant des niveaux proches de 17 dirhams. Une évolution qui, selon l’interlocuteur de Hespress , « reflète les répercussions de la persistance des tensions géopolitiques sur l’économie nationale ». Au-delà du prix des matériaux, la hausse des dépenses de transport et de fonctionnement des engins de chantier alourdit les coûts des opérations immobilières. Dans le segment du logement économique, le coût des travaux réalisés en sous-traitance est ainsi passé de 2.400 à 2.500 dirhams le mètre carré à une fourchette comprise entre 3.000 et 3.200 dirhams, selon des données professionnelles concordantes. À ces contraintes s’ajoutent les difficultés de recrutement et de fidélisation de la main-d’œuvre. Les promoteurs font face à des revendications salariales croissantes, dans un contexte marqué par la hausse du coût de la vie. Les délais administratifs constituent un autre obstacle. L’obtention des autorisations et la lenteur des procédures peuvent prendre entre un an et un an et demi, retardant le lancement des projets et exposant les opérations aux fluctuations des prix pendant cette période. Le logement à 300.000 dirhams de plus en plus difficile à produire La hausse cumulée des charges remet en question la viabilité de certains segments du marché. « Il est devenu quasiment impossible de proposer des appartements à 300.000 dirhams dans les conditions actuelles », estime la source professionnelle interrogée par Hespress . Le coût du foncier et des matériaux ne suffit pas, à lui seul, à expliquer cette difficulté. Les promoteurs doivent également composer avec la multiplication des intervenants, les intérêts bancaires et les frais associés aux procédures administratives, autant de dépenses qui s’accumulent tout au long de la réalisation des projets. Une augmentation des prix de vente pourrait permettre de compenser une partie de ces surcoûts, mais cette solution se heurte aux limites financières des ménages. La faiblesse du pouvoir d’achat restreint la capacité des promoteurs à répercuter intégralement la hausse de leurs coûts sur les acquéreurs. Par ailleurs, la progression des indicateurs de consommation de ciment ne doit pas nécessairement être interprétée comme le signe d’une reprise du marché du logement. Selon la source professionnelle, cette hausse est principalement portée par les grands chantiers et les projets non résidentiels, plutôt que par une amélioration de la demande en logements. Les promoteurs appellent à des mesures fiscales et administratives Face à ces difficultés, les professionnels avancent plusieurs propositions à destination du gouvernement, notamment pour favoriser le développement du logement locatif et soutenir la production de logements économiques. Pour encourager l’investissement locatif, la source interrogée par Hespress préconise d’abord de simplifier les procédures administratives et d’accélérer le traitement judiciaire des litiges liés aux expulsions. L’objectif est de rassurer les investisseurs, en réduisant les incertitudes entourant la mise en location des biens immobiliers. Elle propose également des incitations fiscales en faveur des propriétaires qui destinent leurs biens à la location, notamment une exonération des revenus locatifs inférieurs à 1.500 ou 2.000 dirhams. S’agissant du logement économique, les professionnels estiment que la production de logements dont les prix se situent entre 300.000 et 350.000 dirhams nécessite désormais une intervention de l’État, notamment sous la forme d’exonérations fiscales accordées aux promoteurs immobiliers. La profession se dit enfin disposée à travailler avec les nouvelles autorités gouvernementales et à leur soumettre ses propositions, à condition qu’un dialogue soit engagé. « L’objectif des promoteurs ne se limite pas à la réalisation de bénéfices, mais consiste également à garantir la stabilité sociale et à fournir un logement décent », souligne la source. The post Immobilier : La flambée des coûts de construction met le logement économique sous pression appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Suspected soldiers kill two youths in Ebonyi
items.description: Community demands discreet investigation By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki Tension has gripped Ihetutu community in Ishiagu, Ivo Local Government Area of Ebonyi State, following the alleged killing of two youths by suspected soldiers attached to a mining company in the area. The deceased, identified as Chibuike Elema, 18, and Obinna Joshua, 19, were reportedly shot dead around midday on Sunday at a mining site operated by Palladium Mining Company. According to accounts by residents and the father of one of the victims, the youths were allegedly shot after they declined a demand by the soldiers for money while returning from work. The incident sparked outrage among residents, particularly women and community leaders, who called for an impartial investigation into the killings and raised concerns over the treatment of community members by the mining company and security personnel. There was an atmosphere of grief and tension in the community on Sunday evening when our correspondent visited the area. Narrating the circumstances surrounding his son’s death, Donatus Okoro, father of Chibuike Elema, said his 18-year-old son had been called from home on Sunday morning to join other workers at the mining site. He said eyewitnesses told him that the youths were returning from work when soldiers attached to Palladium Mining Company allegedly demanded money from them. The grieving father alleged that the soldiers opened fire after the youths said they had no money to give them. “My son was called from the house this morning to come and join them for Sunday work. While coming back along the road, according to people who witnessed what happened, the soldiers attached to a mining company called Palladium asked them to settle them. “But they told the soldiers that they were not with anything. The soldiers raised their guns and shot them in the head,” he alleged. Okoro appealed to the Ebonyi State Government to investigate the incident and ensure that anyone found responsible for his son’s death was brought to justice. The second victim, Obinna Joshua, was identified as the son of the serving councillor representing Ihetutu community in Ivo LGA. He was reportedly a second-year undergraduate student. The killings have heightened concerns among residents over the use of lethal force at the mining site. Community leaders maintained that even if the youths were suspected of an offence, they should have been arrested and handed over to the police. The Chairman of the Board of Trustees of Ihetutu Community Development Union, Prince Fabian Chukwu, condemned the incident and urged the state government to intervene. Chukwu described the killings as unacceptable, saying security personnel deployed to protect a mining operation should not take the law into their own hands. “We are not happy. For a miner working in our community to authorise security personnel to kill our youths is something we cannot accept,” he said. “Even if the youths had come to take anything from the company, the appropriate thing would have been to arrest them and hand them over to the police, not to kill them. They were not authorised to kill a vibrant youth like that,” he added. The community leader said Palladium had operated in the area for about five years or more. According to him, the company initially worked as a technical partner to another mining firm before taking over operations at the site. Chukwu alleged that the company’s owner, Victor Nwokeji, had taken over the mining site from Gexpam Mining Company, which he said had brought Nwokeji in as a partner in a lead-zinc concession at Ihetutu. He further alleged that the mining operation was currently being run under the name Ambertone Logistics Ltd, which he described as another arm of Palladium Mining Company. According to Chukwu, tensions between the community and the company had become more pronounced following the change in ownership or operational control. He appealed to the state government to intervene urgently to prevent the situation from escalating, while urging the bereaved families to remain calm as the community seeks justice. Also speaking, Mrs Ifeyinwa Eze, a former secretary of the women’s wing of the Ihetutu Community Development Union, accused the mining company and security personnel of treating residents unfairly. She called for an investigation into the killings and a review of the continued operations of the company and the soldiers in the community. “They are treating our children as if they are thieves. We want them to go. The government should stop both the mining company and the army from operating in Ihetutu. They are treating us like slaves, and it has never been like this before,” she said. Questioning the circumstances surrounding the deaths, Eze said Sunday was a normal working day for male miners in the community, contrary to any suggestion that the youths had committed an offence simply by going to the mining site. “What crime have these children committed by going to the site today? Men work on Sundays; it is only women who do not go to the mining site on Sundays,” she said. The incident has left the community mourning the two young men and raised fresh questions about the conduct of security personnel deployed to protect mining operations. Residents are calling on the Ebonyi State Government and relevant security authorities to conduct an impartial investigation, establish the circumstances surrounding the shootings and ensure that anyone found culpable is held accountable. As the bereaved families mourn their loved ones, community members insist that justice must be served and that measures must be taken to prevent a recurrence. The post Suspected soldiers kill two youths in Ebonyi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Asantehene backs government’s mineral policies, says GoldBod reflects Nkrumah’s vision
items.description: The Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, has backed the government’s mineral policies, including the establishment of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), saying they are helping Ghana take greater control of its mineral resources and retain more value from its gold. Speaking on behalf of the Asantehene at the Mining in Motion Conference, the Essumejahene, Nana Okyere Kusi Ntrama, said the government’s mineral sector reforms reflected a deliberate effort to strengthen state control over the country’s natural resources. He acknowledged the controversies surrounding GoldBod but maintained that they did not undermine the broader direction of the government’s Reset agenda. “Over the past year, the contours of the new agenda have become clear. Whatever we make of the minerals in the ground, the mineral policies of the government, and regardless of the controversies surrounding the GoldBod, there can only be no doubt that the nature of the President’s Reset agenda is intact,” he said. Nana Okyere Kusi Ntrama said the policies demonstrated political courage and brought to mind Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah, and his efforts to place the country’s mineral resources under state control. He recalled Nkrumah’s attempt to establish a gold refinery in Tarkwa, describing it as part of a deliberate effort to ensure Ghana derived greater benefits from its natural resources. “It reflects the political courage of the kind of which only true heroes are gifted. It takes us right back to the very foundation of our republic, when Dr Kwame Nkrumah sought to bring our minerals under the control of the state and moved to establish a gold refinery in Tarkwa,” he said. “Another intentional quest. However, he paid a heavy price for this audacity.” The Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah Kofi Buah, also outlined the government’s plans to reform the mining sector, saying the changes were intended to provide clearer rules for investors, stronger protections for mining communities and a firmer foundation for long-term national development. In his remarks at the conference, the minister said Cabinet had approved a revised Minerals and Mining Policy and endorsed proposed amendments to the Minerals and Mining Act for consideration by Parliament. “Our reforms are intended to give investors clearer rules, communities more dependable protections, and a republic stronger foundation for long-term development,” he said. According to the minister, the proposed changes address licensing, local participation and community development, areas considered important to improving the management of the country’s mineral resources. He also pointed to efforts to increase the value Ghana retains from mineral production, particularly gold from the small-scale mining sector. “The Ghana Gold Board has brought a more organised approach to the purchase and export of small-scale gold,” he said. The minister added that expanding refining capacity, improving gold-testing facilities and strengthening traceability were also important to building a more credible and productive gold value chain. “In addition to these efforts, expanding refining, improving assay capacity, and strengthening traceability are important steps towards a more credible and productive gold value chain,” he said.

items.title: 2027: Yilwatda tasks Lagos APC to deliver Tinubu, Hamzat
items.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni The National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, has charged party leaders and members in Lagos State to ensure the victory of President Bola Tinubu, the party’s governorship candidate, Dr Obafemi Hamzat, and all its candidates in the 2027 general elections. Yilwatda gave the charge on Monday at a one-day retreat for leaders and senior members of the PBAT-KOH Campaign Council, held at Eko Hotel and Suites, Lagos. The retreat, themed “One Roof, One Tent, One Friend, One Shared Responsibility,” focused on party unity, reconciliation, grassroots mobilisation and preparations for the forthcoming elections. The APC national chairman said all party leaders, political appointees and structures must work towards a common goal, warning against placing personal interests above the party’s collective ambition. “When we say we have one team, we simply mean that every leader, every appointee, every party structure must walk towards the bigger mission and vision of the party to win an election. “Anything outside that is personal interest. No single individual, regardless of how influential, can win an election,” he said. Yilwatda said his visit to Lagos was strategic because of the state’s large voting population and the APC’s loss in the state during the 2023 presidential election. “Lagos has over seven million registered voters. It is the centre of commerce, the political nerve of this country. If you win Lagos, you almost won Nigeria. If Lagos speaks, Nigeria speaks,” he said. He added: “Secondly, I’m here because last election we lost Lagos. So I want to speak to Lagosians. This time around, it is our time to deliver Lagos. First to Mr President, and then deliver our Governor, and deliver all our National Assembly members and House of Assembly members. This is a must-do for us.” The national chairman urged party leaders to strengthen their relationships with grassroots supporters and communicate the administration’s achievements more effectively to voters. He also warned against what he described as “elective amnesia”, where voters support candidates at one level of government but fail to vote for other candidates of the same party. “If you vote for Mr President and you don’t have National Assembly, how do we run government? If you vote for Governor and you don’t vote for House of Assembly to concur to constitutional amendments, how do you move forward? APC needs majority in National Assembly and House of Assembly,” he said. Reconciliation, party discipline On internal disagreements, Yilwatda acknowledged that differences and political ambitions were inevitable in a large party but said they should not be allowed to undermine its unity. Citing his political experience, he recalled losing the 2023 governorship election before subsequently serving as a minister and emerging as the APC national chairman. He urged aggrieved members to remain committed to the party, while encouraging leaders to identify dissatisfied members and create room for dialogue and reconciliation. “You may not have it today, but who told you tomorrow is same as yesterday? Work for party, stand for party. Let’s do stakeholder mapping and look at people who are aggrieved. There must be room for dialogue and conciliation,” he said. Yilwatda also warned members against undermining the party’s internal processes because their personal preferences were not reflected in the emergence of candidates. He said party members were expected to support candidates who emerged through its established procedures, regardless of individual disagreements. “Even if you don’t like him, immediately he won election, he is now my candidate. He is now party candidate. Support them because that’s what party has presented,” he said. APC chairman raises concern over polling unit agents The APC national chairman expressed concern over the delay in submitting the list of polling unit agents from Lagos State, warning that the party must avoid a repeat of the difficulties it encountered during the previous election. He said the party had resorted to legal action to complete its agents’ list in the last election and urged Lagos leaders to ensure that all necessary preparations were completed within the stipulated timelines. “Elections end at polling unit. Do you have your agents? I’m yet to receive list of your agents from Lagos. Last election, APC had to go to court to complete list. “This time, we must meet timeline. Why PDP couldn’t take us to court on merit was because they had no agent in most polling units. We shouldn’t be victims of ourselves,” Yilwatda said. He directed party leaders to mobilise 10 canvassers per polling unit and ensure that the agents’ list was digitised and uploaded on time. Tinubu’s projects need better publicity On communication, Yilwatda said the APC needed to do more to publicise the achievements of the Tinubu administration, arguing that some beneficiaries of government projects were unaware of the administration responsible for them. He listed major infrastructure projects, including the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, the proposed Trans-Sahara Highway linking Calabar with northern states, the Sokoto-Badagry Super Highway, the Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano (AKK) gas pipeline project, and the Lagos Blue and Red rail lines. He also highlighted the administration’s tax reforms, which took effect in January 2026, saying the changes had reduced the tax burden on some low-income earners. “So many projects. People are beneficiaries, they don’t even know. Why are we silent? Tell story, sing song. Tell them what APC has done,” he said. Yilwatda maintained that the party was bigger than any individual, including Tinubu and himself, and cited the President’s participation in party screening, primary elections and other internal processes as evidence of the importance of party rules. He urged members to prioritise collective responsibility, strengthen grassroots structures and resolve internal disagreements ahead of the 2027 elections. “Road to ballot requires preparation, patience, honest communication and willingness to put collective responsibility above personal differences. “Let us build structures, strengthen relationships with grassroots, resolve differences. Let’s make Lagos win this time,” he said. The post 2027: Yilwatda tasks Lagos APC to deliver Tinubu, Hamzat appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: How Did Life Arise? Three Turning Points in Early Evolution
No, misdemeanours do attract a prison term in Ghana, even 25 years
items.description: Introduction A few weeks ago, a certain wind began to blow through our legal streets, and it appears to be gaining momentum. It carries a seductive but specious dictum that misdemeanours in Ghana attract no custodial sentence, only a fine; that bail in such cases is a matter of right; and that a judge who refuses it deserves to be rusticated to the classroom. Specious as its momentum may be, and with the greatest respect to its proponents, the statute book tells a more sober story. The law is not swayed by wind. Let us go to the black letter, where the law has built its hospital and labelled its wards. 1. The Nomenclature of Crimes – The Hospital of Section 296, Act 30 Ghana’s criminal jurisprudence is structured like a hospital triage. At the Emergency Ward lie capital offences; at the Intensive Care Unit, first-degree felonies; at the General Ward, second-degree felonies; and at the Out-Patient Department (OPD) lie misdemeanours. The fact that the OPD is at the entrance does not mean it is not part of the hospital. But OPD, too, has beds, and those beds have chains. 2. The Three-Year Bed – Section 296(4) Act 30 Section 296(4) of the Criminal and Other Offences (Procedure) Act, 1960 (Act 30) is the admission register for the OPD. It states in plain language: “Where a criminal offence which is not an offence mentioned in subsection (5), is declared by any enactment to be a misdemeanour and the punishment for the offence is not specified, a person convicted thereof shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years.” (my emphasis). When our elders build a house, they also measure its shadow. Parliament has measured the shadow of the OPD. Its shadow is three (3) years. Nulla poena sine lege – but here, the lex has provided the poena . To say OPD has no beds is to admire the signboard and ignore the ward. Three years is not a slap on the wrist. It is a deprivation of liberty. As Lutterodt, Karimu and Djarbeng have noted that a review of Act 29 reveals that 25 offences are classified as first-degree felonies, 44 offences are classified as second-degree felonies, and 133 offences are classified as misdemeanours. Assault simpliciter (Section 84), offensive conduct conducive to a breach of the peace (Section 207), publication of false news under Section 208(1) of Act 29 – all parade under this shadow of incarceration. They enter through the OPD door, but they sleep on beds with chains. 3. The Lion in a Sheep’s Skin – Section 296(5) Act 30 and the Metamorphosis under Act 1034 Even more striking is Section 296(5). Some misdemeanours have the teeth of a lion. Non nomen, sed poena. Section 296(5) lists fourteen offences with an enhanced ceiling. It provides: “A person convicted of a criminal offence under any of the following sections of the Criminal Code, 1960 (Act 29), that is to say, sections 124, 128, 131, 138, 140, 145, 151, 152, 154, 158, 165, 239, 252, 253 and 260 shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding twenty-five years. “ Of these fourteen, the hospital register reveals two curious discoveries: – Seven are second degree felonies: Sections 124, 128, 131, 138, 151, 152 and 158. Ordinarily, a second-degree felony sleeps on a ten (10)-year bed under Section 296(2). But by reason of Section 296(5) of Act 30, its bed has been elongated. Lex specialis derogate legi generali . By this special provision, they now carry up to twenty-five years. The General Ward patient has been moved to High Dependency. – Seven are, or were misdemeanours : This is the true lion is a sheep’s skin. Section 145 (fraud by agents), Section 154 (possession of instruments for unlawful entry) and Section 165 (possession of means of forging) remain misdemeanours today, yet they carry twenty-five (25) years. They enter through the OPD door, but they sleep on the High Dependency beds. And Section 239 (corruption of and by a public officer or juror), Section 252 (accepting or giving bribe to influence a public officer or juror), Section 253 (corruption promise by a judicial officer or juror) and Section 260 (withholding of a public money by a public officer) were misdemeanours punishable by up to twenty-five (25) years. As the elders say, “The chick that will grow into a cock can be spotted the very day it hatches.” Parliament spotted the gravity of these chicks. Indeed, in 2020, Parliament, by the Criminal Offences (Amendment) Act, 2020 (Act 1034), completed the metamorphosis. It amended Sections 239, 252, 253 and 260 of Act 29 to impose a term of not less than twelve (12) years and not more than twenty-five (25) years upon summary conviction. What does this mean? Mutatis mutandis, the sheep shed its skin. What was once called misdemeanour now carries a mandatory minimum of twelve years. It no longer sleeps in OPD. It has been wheeled by statute, into High Dependency. Act 1034 did not expressly reclassify them as felonies. It primarily introduced a minimum mandatory term of twelve (12) years and retained the twenty-five (25)-year ceiling. Its long title declares the purpose “to categorise the offence of corruption as a felony”, but the operative provisions say only that the offender “commits an offence”, Since there was no reclassification by the amending statute, the four misdemeanours in issue do not technically acquire the incidents of felonies in other wards of the law. What Parliament did not expressly reclassify; the courts must not impliedly reclassify. The long title is the signboard; the operative provision is the ward. But the lesson remains, To say misdemeanours, attract no prison term, therefore, is to ignore that a misdemeanour in Ghana could, until 2020 and even now with offences associated with it, earn you a quarter of a century behind bars. As our elders say, “ A child may be small, but his load may be that of an elder.” A small name, a heavy load. 4. Bail is Not for the Asking – But the Courts Should Be Slow to Refuse Bail in Misdemeanours Bail is not for the asking. Section 96 of Act 30 vests the court with a judicial measuring tape: the likelihood of appearance, the risk of interference with the witnesses or the evidence, the nature and the gravity of the offence, the character and antecedents, and public safety. It is settled practice that a court should be slow to refuse bail in misdemeanour cases, the presumption being in favour of liberty. Libertas omnibus rebus favorabilior est – liberty is favoured above all things. The OPD patient is ordinarily treated and allowed to go home. He is not kept overnight unless his wound is likely to infect others. Slow, however, does not mean “powerless.” Discretio est discernere per legem quid sit justum – discretion is to discern through law what is just. A person charged with a misdemeanour possessing two passports, a one-way ticket to London, and a penchant for intimidating complainants may be justifiably remanded in prison custody. That is not judicial illiteracy. That is judicial fidelity to Section 96. That is the court reading the measuring tape correctly. The court is not bereft of jurisdiction to remand a person charged with a misdemeanour where the Section 96 of Act 30 factors militate against bail. To construe otherwise is to turn discretion into compulsion and the measuring tape into a handcuff on the judge himself. 5. Community Service Act, 2026 (Act 1175) – Four Gates, Not an Open Door The current refrain is that Act 1175 makes community service automatic for all misdemeanours. Act 1175 itself says otherwise. Gate 1 – Discretion and Ceiling – Sections 40 and 41(1) Section 40 : “Where a court convicts an accused person for the commission of misdemeanour or any other offence specified in section 41, the court may , in passing sentence, grant the option of the performance of community service by the convicted person as an alternative punishment.” Section 41(1) : “A community service order made under section 46 applies to an offence punishable by a term of imprisonment of not more than three years with or without the option of a fine.” Section 41(2) then clarifies that for purposes of Section 41(1), it does not matter whether the creating enactment says (a) a fine only, (b) imprisonment only, (c) a fine with the option of imprisonment or (d) a fine and imprisonment. The form is irrelevant; the ceiling of three (3) years is decisive. If your offence is one of the Section 296(5) 25-year offences – whether a second degree felony or a misdemeanour under Sections 145, 154, 165, 239, 252, 253, 260 – you cannot pass Gate 1. The operative word is “may” is permissive, not mandatory. Parliament chose it advisedly. Gate 2 – Summary Trial Filter – Section 42 Section 42: “Despite any provision in an enactment, a court shall not make a community service order in respect of an offence that is unsuitable for summary determination in accordance with section 179 of Act 30.” Gate 3 – Structures and 5-Year Rollout – Section 43 Section 43: The Minister shall, on the advice of the Secretariat, notify the Chief Justice in writing of: (a) districts or communities of the country where arrangements have been made; and (b) the structures that have been put in place for enforcement. “(2) The Minister shall implement community service programmes in all districts in the country within five years of the coming into force of this Act.” The Act was assented to on 26 August 2026. As at 20 August 2026, the Ministry of Interior was still holding stakeholders consultation on a draft implementation plan. The National Community Service Secretariat, Regional and District organs, District Committees, Supervisors, Rehabilitative Fund, tools and electronic case-tracking system are yet to be established. As at the date of writing, no notification under Section 43 has been issued. Without it, a judge has no station to send the convict to. As our elders say, “ You cannot expect a child to fetch water when you have not given him a pot. ” And in law, Lex non cogit ad impossibilia – the law does not compel the impossible. Ubi jus, ibi remedium must also mean Ubi remedium, ibi structura – where there is a remedy, there must be a structure for the remedy. The OPD may have been told to prescribe the new drug, but the dispensary is empty. Until the Section 43 notification arrives, the court is not left without medicine. A misdemeanour remains punishable by imprisonment or a fine or both, the old faithful prescription of the OPD. What the court cannot do today is to prescribe community service where the pharmacy for it has not been stocked. Gate 4 – Conditions Must Be Met First – Sections 44, 45 and 46(1) Even where structures exist, the new drug is not administered like paracetamol. It requires diagnosis. Section 44 – Social Enquiry Report (mandatory): Where a court determines that a community service order should be made under Section 46, it shall, before making the order, direct a community service officer to conduct enquiry into: the circumstances of the case; the character and antecedents of the convicted person and the health status of the person, and report to the court in a prescribed form. This is clinical. The doctor must examine the file before prescribing. The court does not guess; it shall enquire. Audi alteram partem – and Audi etiam corpus – hear the person, hear the body. Can he sweep? Can he stand? What is his history? According to an African proverb, “ You do not shave a man in his absence .” No community service order without a social enquiry report. To do otherwise is to prescribe spectacles without testing the eyes. Section 45 – Conditions: The Court shall have regard to: (a) the need to protect the public; (b) the prevalence of the offence; (c) the likelihood of reform; (d) previous conviction; (e) understanding of the effect; (f) reparation to the victim; (g) the surety; (h) the conduct during bail, and (i) capacity to perform service. These are the vital signs. Before the court writes the prescription for community service, it must take the vital signs of justice. Is the public safe if this man sweeps the market instead of sleeping in cells? Is this offence a fever in the district – prevalent, contagious, demanding, deterrence? Is this soul likely to reform, or will he treat the broom as a joke? Has he been here before – a habitual patient? Does he understand the wound he caused? Has he repaired the victim, or only repaired his own story? Can a surety hold him? How did he behave when the court, in its mercy, granted him bail – did he honour the prescription or tear it? And finally, can his own body carry the load? This is not a checklist to be ticked with a red pen. It is a judicial scale – et trutina, non calamus – a weighing, not merely a writing. The OPD doctor does not prescribe the same drug to the asthmatic and the marathon runner. So too, the court must discern. In the view of our elders, “ The one who will be given a load to carry must first be asked whether he has knees. ” Capacity to perform service – Section 45 (i) – is the knee of the matter. Section 46(1) – Power to make order: “ Where a court is satisfied that the conditions for making a community service order have been met that court may make a community service order as set out in the First Schedule directing the convicted person to perform a community service.” The syntax is telling: “Where… satisfied”, “have been met” “may”. They all connote discretion, not automatic entitlement. Where the law says “may”, there discretion lives. The law has not said “shall sweep”. It says, “where satisfied … may order sweeping”. The bed must be examined, the vital signs taken, the report read, the conditions weighed, and only when the judicial mind is satisfied – truly satisfied – does the hand reach for the new prescription. Conclusion The position is trite: misdemeanour in Ghana has always attracted a prison sentence, a fine or both. Ordinarily, the imprisonment term is up to three (3) years under Section 296(4). For the misdemeanours listed in Section 296(5) – Sections 145, 154, and 165 still, and Sections 239, 252, 253 and 260 until 2020 – the prison term that could be awarded was up to twenty-five (25) years, a ceiling that applies equally to the second-degree felonies listed in the same subsection. In 2020, Act 1034 introduced a minimum term of imprisonment of twelve (12) years for Sections 239, 252, 253 and 260 to twelve (12) years. They were not expressly reclassified as felonies, which suggests that they retain their beds at the OPD, except that they will now spend more years at the crime hospital. Act 1175 does not abolish that custodial regime. It introduces a conditional alternative available only in notified districts, only for offences capped at three (3) years, only after a social enquiry, and only if the judge is satisfied under Section 46(1). A Judge who imposes a custodial sentence for a misdemeanour is therefore not acting contrary to the law. If citizens are discontented, their anger should first be directed at the legal framework. As posited by one writer, “In imposing prison sentences, the Judges are operating within the law. It is the law that needs reform.” That is the whole homily. A judge who sends a misdemeanant to Nsawam for two years has not invented a law. He applied Section 296. He who imposed a fine has applied the same law. Both are operating within the law. Act 1175 does not punish the judge for waiting. It commands patience. Until the Minister notifies under Section 43, until the Social Enquiry Report is ordered under Section 44, until the vital signs under Section 45 are taken, and until judicial satisfaction is attained under Section 46(1), the new treatment cannot be administered. A court should be slow to refuse bail in misdemeanour cases, but it is not bereft of jurisdiction to remand where Section 96 so demands. Four gates must swing open in sequence. If any remains bolted, the three-year bed in the OPD – and, for Sections 145, 154, 165, 239, 252, 253 and 260, the twenty-five-year bed remains occupied. Let us educate the public. Let us not undermine the bench. If the hospital has no bed, you do not beat the nurse. The bench has applied the beds the law has provided. When facilities are fully-installed in the new ward, the bench will gladly admit patients there. See modernghana.com, “We need to train judges on new laws to ensure proper application – Barker-Vormawor, 22 nd September 2026, https://www.modernghana.com/news/152971/we-need-to-train-judges-on-new-laws-to-ensure-prop.html. The death penalty for ordinary crimes was, however, abolished by the Criminal Offences (Amendment) Act, 2023 (Act 1101), passed by Parliament on 25 July 2023 and assented to on 2 August 2023. The only capital offence in our criminal jurisprudence is High Treason which wears a constitutional cloak. Under Section 296(1), a person convicted of an offence declared by an enactment to be a first-degree felony offence is liable to imprisonment for life or any lesser term. See Section 296(2). See Section 296(4). Her Worship Georgette Carmel Lutterodt, Her Worship Anastacia Yaa Agyeiwaa Karimu and Her Worship Dromo Ahfarley Djarbeng, “Sentencing in the Ghanaian Criminal Justice System: Reconciling Sections 296 and 297 of Act 30 with the Criminal Offences Act”.criminal Law Blog Ghana, 18 February 2026. Selasi Kuwornu, “Non-Custodial Sentences in Ghana”; Ghana Law Hub, December 10, 2018.

items.title: Adebayo condemns Plateau killings, demands urgent action
items.description: By John Alechenu, Abuja The 2027 presidential candidate of the Social Democratic Party (SDP), Prince Adewole Adebayo, has condemned the renewed killings in Plateau State and other parts of the country, calling on Governor Caleb Mutfwang to take urgent steps to protect residents. Adebayo also criticised the Federal Government’s handling of insecurity, accusing President Bola Tinubu’s administration of failing to respond adequately to the security challenges facing the country. His position was contained in a statement issued in Abuja on Monday by Comrade Mark Adebayo, Chief Media and Communications Adviser to the Adebayo-Bugaje Presidential Campaign Council. The SDP candidate expressed grief over the killings in Plateau State, saying hundreds of people had reportedly been killed in attacks across communities between January and October 2026. He said the victims were individuals whose deaths had devastated families and communities, urging the authorities to take decisive action to prevent further loss of lives. “These are not just mere statistics; they are fathers, mothers, sons, and daughters whose lives have been violently cut short while their government stands by in criminal docility,” he said. Adebayo also criticised an earlier engagement by the Plateau State governor with residents affected by insecurity, recalling that Mutfwang had addressed traumatised citizens from inside an armoured personnel carrier. He described the incident as disrespectful to victims and their grieving families, arguing that public officials should demonstrate visible leadership and reassure communities affected by violence. “A leader cannot be hiding in an armoured tank while his people are being slaughtered daily like chickens on the very soil they call home,” he said. The SDP candidate called for an end to the killings, urging the state and federal governments to deploy available resources and security measures to protect vulnerable communities. “The time for empty press statements and crocodile tears is over. Stop the killings now! You have the apparatus, you have the resources, and you have the constitutional backing. Stop the killings because you can — if only you possess the political will to do so,” he said. The campaign council expressed solidarity with families affected by the attacks and called for immediate action to restore peace in Plateau State and other troubled parts of the country. Adebayo said insecurity remained a major obstacle to economic development, arguing that people could not engage fully in productive activities without adequate protection. He added that his proposed security blueprint focused on strengthening security institutions, restoring government control over affected territories and addressing the underlying socioeconomic factors contributing to crime. “The security and welfare of the people form the baseline of all government actions. Without security, there can be no meaningful production; without production, there can be no sustainable prosperity,” he said. items.title: Digital tracking helps NPA verify UPPF claims by oil marketers – NPA CEO
items.description: The Chief Executive of the National Petroleum Authority (NPA), Edudzi Tamakloe, says the deployment of technology since 2020 has helped reduce human interference in the determination and payment of claims under the UPPF to Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs). Speaking before the Public Accounts Committee on October 19, Mr Tamakloe explained that the technological systems introduced over the period had helped the NPA verify claims more accurately, ensuring that payments made to OMCs reflected eligible transactions and the actual movement of bulk road vehicles transporting petroleum products. “In 2020, the then chief executive and the board at that time decided that there was a need to introduce technology to help in ensuring that funds are adequately protected,” he told the Committee. According to him, the adoption of technology has improved the authority’s ability to validate claims and minimise opportunities for human interference in a process that previously depended, in part, on physical verification by personnel. “The introduction of technology over the period has helped in ensuring that we pay appropriate claims,” he said. Mr Tamakloe said one of the significant benefits of the technological systems was their ability to establish whether petroleum products transported by bulk road vehicles reached the destinations declared by the companies involved. Under the previous arrangement, personnel from the Bureau of National Investigations (BNI) were used to undertake physical verification exercises to establish whether vehicles had reached their stated destinations. Mr Tamakloe indicated that although the verification process was intended to ensure that claims were legitimate, its reliance on human interaction created opportunities for inconsistencies and possible interference. “The human interface had the potential of coming out with all kinds of stuff,” he said. The NPA chief executive suggested that replacing or reducing reliance on such manual checks through technology had helped strengthen the integrity of the process by providing more direct and timely information about vehicle movements. With digital tracking, he said, the authority could monitor the movement of bulk road vehicles from the point at which a journey began until they arrived at their final destinations. This, he explained, enabled the NPA to verify claims against recorded movements rather than relying solely on physical checks or information supplied by the parties involved. He also indicated that the system incorporated a mechanism to regulate or flag tampering, helping the authority monitor the integrity of the tracking process. Such monitoring is intended to make it more difficult for claims to be processed on the basis of journeys that cannot be substantiated by the available tracking information. Mr Tamakloe, however, attributed the improvements not to technology alone but also to the work of the authority’s management committee and other personnel involved in administering the fund. “So together, the deployment of technology, the work of the management committee and others have resulted in the kind of situation that we have now,” he said. He added that the system provided an essential basis for transactions involving OMCs, stressing that companies could not deal with the authority without being registered on the relevant portal. “So you cannot, for an OMC, deal without the benefit of being on that,” he said. The explanation highlighted the importance of the NPA’s digital infrastructure in administering its regulatory responsibilities, monitoring transactions and supporting the verification of claims submitted under the UPPF. Implications for accountability and fund protection The UPPF is a mechanism within Ghana’s petroleum pricing framework that supports the application of uniform petroleum prices across the country, helping to address differences in transportation costs between locations. The verification of transportation activities is therefore important to the administration of claims associated with moving petroleum products from one part of the country to another. The NPA’s use of technology, as outlined by Mr Tamakloe, is intended to strengthen the checks applied to such claims by providing verifiable information on vehicle movements and transactions. The system also reduces dependence on manual verification, which can be time-consuming and may expose the process to inconsistencies or undue influence. For the authority, the ability to monitor vehicles from the beginning to the end of their journeys provides an additional means of checking whether the transportation activities underpinning claims correspond with recorded movements. The requirement for OMCs to use the NPA’s portal also establishes a common digital framework through which transactions can be monitored, supporting the authority’s oversight of companies operating in the downstream petroleum sector. However, while Mr Tamakloe said the introduction of technology had helped reduce human interference and improve the accuracy of claims, his remarks did not provide figures on the extent of the reduction, the amount of money saved or the number of claims rejected following the introduction of the systems. Neither did the account of his remarks establish the precise financial impact of the technology on the fund’s overall performance. Technology and management reforms credited for current system Mr Tamakloe’s appearance before the Public Accounts Committee placed the NPA’s technological reforms at the centre of discussions about the verification of claims and the protection of public funds within the petroleum sector. His account suggested that the changes introduced in 2020 were intended to address weaknesses associated with manual verification while providing the authority with more reliable information for assessing transportation-related claims. By combining real-time vehicle tracking, transaction monitoring through its enterprise relational database and the work of its management committee, the NPA says it has strengthened the processes used to determine appropriate payments to OMCs. The requirement for OMCs to be registered on the authority’s portal further ensures that the companies operate within the NPA’s digital regulatory framework. Mr Tamakloe’s testimony therefore highlighted the authority’s reliance on technology as an important component of its efforts to protect the UPPF, improve accountability and ensure that payments are based on claims that can be properly verified. The extent to which these measures have translated into measurable financial savings or a quantified reduction in irregular claims, however, remains to be established through further data from the authority.

No further action against government adviser’s wife over Palestine Action post, police say
items.description: Police say no further action will be taken against the wife of the government’s national security adviser after she posted on social media referencing Palestine Action. Sarah Helm, who is married to Jonathan Powell, wrote on X on Thursday: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.” She was responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support the proscribed organisation. On Saturday, the Metropolitan Police said Helm’s post was “assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold”. “No further police action will be taken,” the force added. On Friday, the Met Police had said it was “in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required” after it was “made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action”. Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025. Support of the group is a criminal offence and punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Best-selling author Rooney said she would donate earnings from her books to the group, which has a stated goal of “ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. As a result, Rooney’s publisher, Faber, determined it could not sell her novels, including Normal People and Conversations with Friends, in the UK.

items.title: Bomb threat forces Israel to Austria flight into emergency landing
items.description: An Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria was forced to divert to Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat. The Airbus A320 plane was travelling from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday night but made an emergency landing in Sofia, where passengers were evacuated, the Bulgarian transport ministry said in a statement. The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner, the statement said. No injuries have been reported and an investigation has begun. It comes after a pilot attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight en route to Tel Aviv last month by attacking the captain, before the flight’s crew and passengers overpowered him and landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia. Bulgarian and Israeli media reported that a bomb threat had been made. Austrian Airlines confirmed a threat was made, without giving further details. A spokesperson told the BBC there were 51 passengers and six crew members on board the jet. Authorities conducted a security search of the plane after it landed in Sofia, about 30 minutes from when the alert was first raised. It was over Romania when it diverted to Sofia. Austrian Airlines confirmed that no threat was found and the flight finished its journey to Vienna with all passengers on board. Flight tracking data showed Austrian Airlines 82 left Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday evening before landing at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia three hours later. Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert.

items.title: High cost of farm inputs driving tomato prices — TOOPAN
items.description: …Plans solar dryers to reduce post-harvest losses By Gabriel Ewepu ABUJA — The National President of the Tomatoes and Orchard Producers Association of Nigeria (TOOPAN), Oyeleke Bola, has attributed the high prices of tomatoes across the country to the rising cost of farm inputs. Bola, who spoke with Vanguard over the weekend, said tomato farmers were grappling with increasing production costs and called for government support to boost output and improve affordability. He said the depreciation of the naira against the dollar had increased the cost of agricultural inputs, particularly seeds, making tomato production more expensive. “The cost of production per hectare is high now. The amount we spend on production is no longer the same as what we used to spend, owing to the high cost of foreign exchange resulting from the increase in the dollar-to-naira exchange rate. “Seeds are currently very expensive. Tomato farmers used to buy seeds for between N20,000 and N25,000, but now they cost between N35,000 and N40,000. “Fertiliser costs are also on the high side. Generally, the cost of production is very high. The Bank of Agriculture is helping us with fertiliser, so there is some cushioning effect on fertiliser costs and other farm inputs,” he said. Despite the challenges, Bola said the association was working to increase production by improving yields and helping farmers access better-quality seeds. “We are working very hard to ensure that we increase production, particularly by raising yields from 25 tonnes to 80 tonnes per hectare. The leadership of the association is also working tirelessly, travelling to identify better seeds that small-scale farmers can use to increase production. “We are also exploring opportunities that can attract investors. To this end, we are travelling outside the country to source good-quality seeds,” he said. On government support for the tomato value chain, Bola said interventions were being provided through the Bank of Agriculture, the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN) and the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security. “People may say it is late, but at least it is coming at the right time because farmers need it. We need it to increase production. So, we are working very hard,” he said. Bola also announced that TOOPAN would hold its Third National Tomato Conference in Abuja from November 26 to 27, 2026, with stakeholders across the tomato value chain expected to participate. He said the conference would focus on strategies to increase production, improve irrigation systems, promote land preparation and tractorisation, and encourage industrialisation in the sector. On post-harvest losses, the TOOPAN president said the association was exploring processing and preservation technologies to reduce waste and improve the value of harvested tomatoes. “We are doing a lot to reduce post-harvest losses. We are working on several initiatives, including exploring opportunities in the tomato paste industry, solar dryers and hydro dryers,” he said. He explained that the association was considering establishing solar-drying facilities in up to 16 states to help farmers preserve their produce and create opportunities for women involved in processing. “We are looking at the entire value chain to ensure that we can convert waste into finished products. We are working towards establishing solar dryers in up to 16 states across the country and setting them up in different regions. We intend to establish hubs where women can use the facilities to reduce post-harvest losses,” he said. According to Bola, research institutions under the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security are working on solar-drying technologies to reduce post-harvest losses and support exports. He added that the African Union was also exploring possible investment in the initiative, while the association was seeking private-sector investors to support the development of processing and preservation facilities across the country. The post High cost of farm inputs driving tomato prices — TOOPAN appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Digital Governmentality in Africa
items.description: The concept of governmentality refers to the practice through which behaviours of population are directed, constrained, and framed. The concept was originally appeared in the work of a popular sociologist, Michel Foucault’s “logics of power ” to denote guiding the possibility of conduct and putting in order the possible outcome and to understand how governments control over their populations through policy instruments, arithmetic and algorithmic control, preventing or making them to act in a certain way. Digital governmentality denotes ways of leading users’ behaviours online, by designing technical resources, directing, constraining and framing.” Some writers use a narrower concept of algorithmic governmentality , which refers to the increasing reliance on algorithmic regulation, predictive analytics, datafication, and automated decision‑making rather than the traditional models of governance, which relied on paper-based services, laws, coercion, and ideological state apparatuses. The rise of the internet boom, mobile communication revolution, and artificial intelligence (AI) in the modern world is shaping how people behave, learn, work, and live. The introduction of the internet created a global platform of communication and business for people, governments, and private entities. This was further accelerated by the transformation through mobile communication technologies, where the introduction of smartphones rapidly changed the behavior of people. These improvements increased speed, certainty, reliability, connectivity, collaboration, innovations, and productivity of services. Recently, AI, advanced data computing power, deep learning technologies, and machine learning are accelerating the transformation of societies. The expansion of these technologies has created unprecedented opportunities for governments to improve the delivery of public services. They enabled governments to digitize information and services, making it easier for citizens to access forms, licenses, tax services, and public records online. The widespread adoption of mobile technologies further extended this reach, enabling people to interact with government services anytime and anywhere through smartphones and mobile applications. Currently, AI has been introduced making government institutions more responsive, and data-driven, by analyzing large volumes of information, automating routine administrative tasks, supporting decision-making, and delivering personalized services to citizens. Recently, AI and digital technologies have been a key priority agenda of Africa. The continent adopted a Continental AI Strategy in 2024. A High Level Policy Dialogue was convened by the AU on the development and regulation of AI in Africa on 17 May 2025 where commitments have been reflected to integrate AI in their development agenda. Currently, 22 countries in the continent developed their own AI strategy . For instance, Ethiopia adopted a National AI policy in 2024, and established the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute (EAII) in 2020 to expand the application of AI in key sectors including healthcare, agriculture, education, and defense. Following this, various actions took place. For instance, the Digital Ethiopia 2025-2030 Strategy was one of the key actions taken in expanding digital infrastructure and e-government platforms. Ghana also developed a national AI Strategy (2025-35) focusing on youth jobs, education, data governance, applied research, community ecosystem, and public sector governance. The country also proposed the establishment of an autonomous organ responsible for overseeing ethical compliance. Kenya also adopted a 2025-30 AI strategy in March 2025 focusing on expanding digital infrastructure, data governance, research, innovation and commercialization. Digital governmentality sets the critical lens to discuss how digital tools direct, constrain, and frame behavior and provides the context for subsequent policy analysis on digital authoritarianism, technological sovereignty, surveillance concerns, and loss of human agency. Despite contributing in improving the speed and accessibility of many of the essential public services all over Africa, it is also increasingly important to debate concerning politicization, state control, ethics and privacy, and freedom of expression. Critics present cases related to each of such challenges. For example, some analysts mention ‘data and technological sovereignty’, where almost all of the technologies being used to make the analysis and predictions are owned by foreign companies, and the data being collected and stored for use in decision making are vulnerable to various external risks. Others like Kebede and Pohjonen (2006) also describe ‘digital authoritarianism’, which refers to the use of digital technologies by governments to monitor, control political activities, and mass surveillance systems, not only to improve public services but also to limit political opposition and restrict freedom of expression. Illustrative manifestation of digital governmentality in some African countries includes ‘Data Boys’ in Nigeria and ‘Media/Digital Army’ in Ethiopia, where governments and political actors informally mobilize media operators and influencers to shape public opinion and counter opposition. Moreover, in Ethiopia, many people also [mis]interpret the Fayda digital identification system as a government policing tool rather than as a neutral modernization project. Social media posts and civil society commentary highlight fears that biometric registration will be used to track political activity, and expand surveillance capacity. Data injustice and inequality is also another key aspect of challenges, including rural-urban divide and socio-economic factors in creating differences in accessing digital services. Another emerging concern is excessive reliance on digital technologies and AI undermines human potential, denoting what Weiskopf and Hansen (2023) called ‘mechanic enslavement’, when everything is reduced to procedures driven by machines, an entirely different form of capture of subjectivity, the individual is considered as ‘cog’ or ‘gear’ of a machinic assemblage, and where ‘quantification’, ‘datafication’ and automation have limited human reflexivity and reduce the capacity to enact responsibility in decision making. This system transforms people into datafied objects, where decisions are made based on algorithmic data rather than lived realities, resulting in the inapplicability of reflexivity and accountability. A body of social media posts have also talked of defects such as some uncertainty and bias in AI systems due to the problem with the data used to train the AI/machine. For instance, AI‑enabled drones have been introduced for both developmental and security purposes. However, there is a public concern that the drones used to monitor protests or communities, reinforcing authoritarian control, and are associated with indiscriminate targeting of civilians. In conclusion, while digital tools are rapidly expanding across the continent and enhancing public service delivery, they operate in a weak regulatory system and the attention given to the ethics and governance aspect is very low. There are limited legal and institutional frameworks designed to prevent, detect, and regulate the misuse of digital technologies, including issues related to misinformation, data exploitation, unethical digital practices, and become vulnerable to manipulation for political or other ends. Furthermore, African countries lack a strong and independent regulatory body with sufficient authority and capacity to effectively monitor and address ethical, privacy, and data protection concerns including those domestically owned and externally controlled digital media platforms. items.title: NDC shifts presidential campaign council inauguration to October 26
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has shifted the unveiling and inauguration of its Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) from October 20 to October 26, 2026. The party’s National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director, announced the change in a statement on Monday, attributing it to the tight schedule of its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, ahead of the 2027 general elections. Director said Obi had an important overseas engagement, necessitating the rescheduling of the event. “The NDC Leadership has announced a new date for the unveiling and inauguration of its National Campaign Council (NCC) earlier slated for Tuesday, 20th October, 2026. “The event will now be held on Monday, 26th October, 2026. “The shift is occasioned by the very tight schedule of our Presidential Candidate, His Excellency, Mr. Peter Obi, who has a very important engagement overseas,” the statement said. The party apologised for any inconvenience caused by the change and urged its members and supporters to remain focused on securing victory for Obi and other NDC candidates in the forthcoming elections. It added: “A New Nigeria is POssible!” The rescheduling comes after the party’s National Chairman, Senator Moses Cleopas, explained the delay in constituting the campaign council during a press briefing on October 10. Cleopas had said the party leadership was consulting Obi and its vice-presidential candidate, Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, on key appointments to ensure that the process was properly handled. He also disclosed that the party had developed the organogram for the campaign council and planned to inaugurate it on October 20. According to him, the event would also feature the presentation of certificates of return to the party’s candidates and a dinner aimed at strengthening cooperation among them ahead of the elections. Cleopas cautioned against rushing the appointment of campaign officials, saying the party needed individuals whose loyalty and commitment would remain firm throughout the electioneering period. “It is not today you are going to have one DG of your campaign and in the middle of the campaign you will hear that your DG is one leg in NDC, one leg somewhere else. It will jeopardise the whole hope of this country,” he said. The post NDC shifts presidential campaign council inauguration to October 26 appeared first on Vanguard News .
