items.title: How Corruption Got This Bad
items.description: “Isn’t that illegal?” That’s a question I get asked a lot as a former federal prosecutor. Donald Trump, his family, and members of his administration are most often the inspiration. Last year, the Qataris gave the U.S. Defense Department a $400 million luxury jumbo jet for the president’s use, which he plans to take with him to his presidential library when he leaves office. Then Trump gave Qatar NATO-like security guarantees. Does that sound like a bribe? Exactly four days before Trump was inaugurated for the second time, the Emiratis invested $500 million in the Trump-family crypto business. Four months later, Trump green-lighted selling them advanced AI chips, which the Biden administration had blocked out of fear that they would fall into the hands of the Chinese. Same question. But even though I hear “Isn’t that illegal?” a lot more than I used to, it isn’t a new question. Former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy and former Virginia Governor Robert McDonnell, a Democrat and a Republican, both took lavish gifts from individuals and entities seeking their help and made national news when they were prosecuted for it. Surely that was illegal? Common sense notwithstanding, however, the answer is no . Neither Espy nor McDonnell were held accountable, and even Trump’s seemingly egregious misbehavior likely can’t be prosecuted. That’s because starting in the 1980s, the Supreme Court has interpreted anti-corruption laws in ways so narrow as to effectively legalize flat-out corruption. These decisions put whole categories of politicians’ conduct beyond a prosecutor’s reach. It’s an absurd result. But we live in the Court’s world. For 20 years, I prosecuted white-collar crime at the U.S. Department of Justice. My first criminal trial was Enron. My last was Hunter Biden. In between, I prosecuted on corruption charges the vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; the mayor of Baltimore; the Baltimore police commissioner; the Baltimore City state’s attorney; and dozens of other politicians, government employees, police officers, and prison guards. I served in leadership positions at the Justice Department and on Capitol Hill focused on corruption. I finished my DOJ career in the department’s Public Integrity Section in Washington, the specialized unit that prosecuted public corruption around the country—until February 2025, when it was effectively shut down. I was one of the prosecutors asked to dismiss the case against New York Mayor Eric Adams. Like nearly all my colleagues in Public Integrity, I declined to do so and left the department that year. In all that time, I experienced how the Supreme Court restrained prosecutors in cases involving public officials. Even before the start of my career, the justices had begun to chip away at federal anti-corruption statutes, and this project accelerated during my tenure. When FBI agents brought me evidence of misconduct, I often had to turn the cases away, knowing I’d never be able to make charges stick. The longer I served, the harder my job became. [ Adam Serwer: Trump’s politicized prosecutions may hit a roadblock ] The first of these Supreme Court rulings was McNally v. United States , decided in 1987. In that case, a member of the Kentucky governor’s Cabinet, a local businessman, and a former chair of the Kentucky Democratic Party received hundreds of thousands of dollars in kickbacks from an insurance company that did business with the state. Prosecutors charged them with depriving the public of its right to their “honest services,” a crime under the federal mail- and wire-fraud statutes. The Court reversed their convictions and declared that the public enjoyed no such right. Although federal courts had upheld similar convictions for more than 40 years, the Supreme Court ruled that all those courts had gotten it wrong: It declared that the mail-fraud—and, by implication, the wire-fraud—statute was limited to protecting money and property, not intangible rights such as citizens’ right to good government. Congress reacted swiftly. One year later, a broad bipartisan majority in Congress passed legislation effectively reversing the Court’s decision. But McNally is an outlier in that regard. In 1999, in United States v. Sun-Diamond Growers of California , the Supreme Court reversed the conviction of an agricultural trade association that gave gifts—tickets to the U.S. Open, expensive luggage, even a crystal bowl—to the U.S. secretary of agriculture in the Clinton administration. The Supreme Court held that giving a politician lavish gifts because of his official position was not illegal. Rather than focusing on the conduct at hand, Justice Antonin Scalia, writing for a unanimous Court, spun out a ridiculous hypothetical—that the government’s interpretation of the statute would allow the president to be prosecuted for accepting “replica jerseys given by championship sports teams.” What that claim ignored was the reality that no Justice Department would ever authorize such a prosecution. In Skilling v. United States , decided in 2010, the Supreme Court reversed the conviction of Jeffrey Skilling, a former CEO of Enron Corporation, for conspiring to commit honest-services fraud. I had been one of the prosecutors in Skilling’s trial. Although Skilling was the president of a publicly traded company, not a politician, he was charged with conspiracy to commit honest-services wire fraud for undisclosed self-dealing. Self-dealing is a problem whether the perpetrator is a corporate executive hiding a conflict of interest from shareholders or an elected official hiding one from voters. Except the Supreme Court held that it wasn’t illegal. Confronted with the fact that lower courts had for years upheld honest-services-fraud convictions for undisclosed self-dealing, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s majority opinion noted the “infrequency” of those decisions and how they were not “models of clarity.” That, of course, didn’t mean those decisions were wrong. Remarkably, Ginsburg didn’t even say they were. Instead, she claimed that because bribery and kickbacks were the “basis of most honest-services prosecutions,” that’s what the statute’s application would be limited to. In place of legal analysis, the Court resorted to a game of numbers, and the practical effect was to restrict the number of corruption cases prosecutors could bring under this statute. In perhaps its grossest pro-corruption decision, the Supreme Court in 2016 reversed Robert McDonnell’s conviction. A jury had convicted the former governor on bribery charges for accepting $175,000 in loans and gifts from the CEO of a nutritional-supplement company that wanted Virginia’s public universities to run clinical trials on his product. The Court held that what McDonnell did for the CEO—setting up meetings, hosting events, talking to other elected officials, all to benefit his company—did not qualify as “official acts,” for which McDonnell could be bribed. Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for a unanimous Court, adopted the most restrictive of definitions of official acts , things such as voting in the Senate or in an official committee. The decision leads directly to the question Why would a CEO give a governor that much money if these weren’t official acts? The Supreme Court didn’t offer an answer. Then, in 2024, in Snyder v. United States , the Supreme Court reversed the conviction of the mayor of Portage, Indiana, for accepting $13,000 from a company that got more than $1 million in city contracts. Prosecutors charged him with violating a statute Congress had enacted to protect federal money administered by the states, called “666,” after its numbering in the United States Code. The indictment had charged these payments to the mayor as illegal gratuities, which is what the law calls “illegal gifts.” In reversing his conviction, the Court held that 666 covered only bribery, not gratuities. In that year alone, approximately $1 trillion in federal funds flowed to the states. As Justice Brett Kavanaugh noted in his majority opinion, as many as 19 million state and local officials administer this money. But according to the Supreme Court, there’s nothing wrong with giving them a little something extra for the effort. That same year, the Court decided Trump v. United States , announcing a sweeping and previously unrecognized doctrine of official-acts immunity for former presidents. Whereas the decisions discussed above left prosecutors room to pursue certain kinds of corruption, the Trump ruling means that presidents, alone among elected officials, can likely never be prosecuted for corruption. That’s because the Court, with Chief Justice Roberts writing for the majority, held that former presidents enjoy absolute immunity for actions within their “core” constitutional authority and presumptive immunity for all other official acts. And worse, unlike the earlier decisions that interpreted statutes and that therefore Congress can reverse by passing new legislation, the Court claimed that presidential immunity was required by the Constitution itself. So only a future Supreme Court that decided to reverse the Trump decision, or an amendment to the Constitution, could cancel the get-out-of-jail-free card the Court gave presidents. [ David Frum: The Trump presidency’s world-historical heist ] All but the last two decisions, Snyder and Trump , spanned the Court’s conservative-liberal divide. Sun-Diamond and McDonnell were even unanimous. This isn’t partisan politics; it’s political elites protecting political elites. The facts in these cases were egregious, but the Court purported to be saving hapless bureaucrats from overzealous prosecutors in the future. In any event, they haven’t. Instead they’ve told juries of ordinary Americans that what they concluded to be corruption was not. Perhaps to try to obscure what it was doing, the Court used technical rather than normative language, something the Fordham law professor Zephyr Teachout explored more broadly in her paper “Demoralizing Elite Fraud,” in The Yale Law Journal . But that technical language can’t obscure the underlying badness of the conduct that the Court blessed. Congress can undo much of what the Supreme Court has done: address Sun-Diamond by making it illegal to give a politician gifts because of his position; address Skilling by designating undisclosed conflicts of interest as honest-services fraud; address McDonnell by expanding the definition of official acts in the bribery statute to cover what politicians actually do all day; and address Snyder by amending 666 to cover gratuities. As noted above, Congress already reversed the Court’s decision in McNally , and prosecutors have brought hundreds of honest-services prosecutions ever since, albeit with the limitations the Skilling decision imposed. Addressing Trump v. United States is tougher, but options still exist: Congress could close off the avenues a president can use to enrich himself and try to build his legacy by, for example, prohibiting the U.S. government from accepting gifts such as the Qatari plane, or disqualifying companies that invest in a president’s businesses or donate to his library from bidding on government contracts. That would be a good first step, but more ambitious approaches are needed, such as Senator Elizabeth Warren’s Anti-Corruption and Public Integrity Act. Unfortunately, Congress, like the Supreme Court, has so far chosen to protect political elites—in Congress’s case, by doing nothing. This behavior should be illegal because corruption is poison to democracy. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote in dissent in Snyder , “Greed makes governments—at every level—less responsive, less efficient, and less trustworthy from the perspective of the communities they serve.” And Americans know it. Results of a Gallup survey announced last month show that Americans’ perceptions of government corruption are at their highest in 20 years: 89 percent of adults say it is widespread. That is a 10-percentage-point increase since 2025 and includes strong majorities of both Democrats and Republicans. Although the Court has placed politicians beyond the law’s reach, at least for now, the public gets it. Hopefully, a new Congress will too.

items.title: The Perfect Liberal
items.description: In 1989, the year the West won the Cold War, Francis Fukuyama published an essay announcing “the end of history.” He wasn’t claiming that historic events would stop taking place; what was over, rather, was the debate about the meaning of those events. Since the Enlightenment, Western thinkers had believed that history was progressing toward a final destination. According to communism, the engine of progress was class conflict, and history would end in the creation of a classless society. With the failure of the Soviet empire, Fukuyama argued, this idea had been discredited. Only one alternative remained: It was now clear that the “end point of mankind’s ideological evolution” was “the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government.” There would still be disagreements within liberalism—Fukuyama named religion and nationalism as likely fault lines—but there could no longer be any disagreement about liberalism. To see how that judgment is holding up, just look at the kinds of titles that political theorists are producing these days: How Liberalism Failed , A World After Liberalism , Liberalism Against Itself . Even Fukuyama wrote a book titled Liberalism and Its Discontents . Across the West, the far right and the far left are on the rise, and the one thing they agree on is their contempt for liberalism. To MAGA and its European cousins, such as France’s National Rally and the United Kingdom’s Reform Party, liberals are rootless elitists who look down on their fellow citizens while coddling immigrants and criminals. To progressives and democratic socialists, liberalism—often qualified with the prefix neo —means ruthless globalized capitalism, prettied up with rhetoric about meritocracy and human rights. Appeals to liberal principles and defenses of the liberal world order have shown little power to rally the public, or even much of the political establishment. Now that the liberal triumphalism of the post–Cold War era is dying, what can replace it? The answer may lie in another important essay written in 1989—one that received much less attention than Fukuyama’s, but enjoys a cult reputation among keepers of the liberal flame. “The Liberalism of Fear,” by Judith Shklar, has just been published for the first time as a book—a small book, because the essay is only about 8,000 words long, but a timely one. In fact, as the political scientist Mark Lilla says in his introduction, it’s “far more timely today than it was upon its publication.” In 1989, Shklar’s minimalist definition of liberalism as a bulwark against government terror—what she calls, simply, a politics of “damage control”—might have sounded unambitious or uninspiring. In an America where ICE agents shoot protesters and grab people off the street, it sounds prescient. Shklar’s argument involves history and philosophy, but like all political ideas, it begins with an intuition, a feeling. Communism, one might say, begins in indignation: a refusal to accept a world where some people exploit and others are exploited. Nationalism begins in loyalty: a sense of connection and obligation to one’s own people. There is nothing wrong with these emotions; they are even praiseworthy. But when one political feeling crowds out all others—when everyone and everything is subordinated to the pursuit of social justice or national pride—good can justify the worst evils. [ From the May 2022 issue: There is no liberal world order ] What makes liberalism different from these political ideologies is that, as Shklar writes, it “does not have any particular positive doctrines about how people are to conduct their lives.” Liberalism doesn’t offer a vision of a perfect world—one where injustice is abolished, or where a particular nation reigns supreme. Instead, it is rooted in a justified fear of the real world, where people with power often use it to oppress, torture, and kill. “Liberalism’s deepest grounding,” Shklar writes, is the belief “that cruelty is an absolute evil.” The classic liberal principles outlined by thinkers such as Locke and Mill, the ideas that guided the American and French Revolutions, follow from this basic fear of cruelty. Freedom of religion means that you won’t be burned at the stake for holding the wrong beliefs. Freedom of speech means that you won’t be locked up for saying what you think. The rule of law means that you can be punished only for committing a crime, not because a powerful person is out to get you. Not coincidentally, these liberal freedoms are framed as limits on the power of the state. “Public cruelty,” Shklar writes, “is made possible by differences in public power,” and the government is always more powerful than any citizen. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing; we want the government to have the power to punish crime or defend against invasion. But liberalism believes that there must be strict and effective limits on how that power is used. “The governments of this world, with their overwhelming power to kill, maim, indoctrinate, and make war are not to be trusted unconditionally,” Shklar writes. What the liberalism of fear wants to prevent above all are “habitual and pervasive acts of cruelty and torture performed by military, paramilitary, and police agents in any regime.” This might have seemed like an odd concern for an American political philosopher in 1989. Police states were disappearing in Eastern Europe; democracy activists were bravely standing up to tanks in Tiananmen Square; Nelson Mandela left his jail cell on his way to becoming president of South Africa. America under George H. W. Bush had its problems, but no one would have put paramilitary violence and police torture high on the list. At a time when Fukuyama was celebrating the end of history, why was Shklar contemplating these specters at the feast? The most obvious answer is that, unlike most Americans, she had seen them firsthand. Born to a Jewish family in Latvia in 1928, Judith Nisse grew up in the shadow of approaching war and the Holocaust. In an autobiographical lecture, she recalled that as a child, she was traumatized by reading Shakespeare’s play Titus Andronicus , which is full of murder, cannibalism, and severed heads: “To this day I can still feel the fear and horror it inspired.” Her sister tried to comfort her by saying that “these things did not really happen,” but it didn’t help, because “both she and I knew that far worse was going on all around us.” As Jews in Latvia, Shklar recalled, “everyone around us wanted us to be somewhere else at best, or to kill us at worst.” The Nisse family managed to escape at the last possible moment and took an epic journey in 1940 across Russia and the Pacific to Canada. The next year, the Nazis invaded Latvia and the 40,000 Jews of Riga were murdered, most of them shot by German troops and local auxiliaries in a nearby forest. When Shklar arrived at Harvard’s department of government as a graduate student in 1951, she was struck by how completely her American colleagues ignored the central political experience of their own time: “I knew what had happened in Europe between 1940 and 1945, and I assumed that most people at Harvard also were aware of the physical, political, and moral calamity that had occurred, but it was never to be discussed.” This “isolating” experience “had a lot to do with my later writings,” Shklar noted. At first, she didn’t intend to stay in the academy: “I would have liked to be a literary editor of The Atlantic or some such publication.” But she remained at Harvard for her entire career as a professor, writing about subjects directly or indirectly connected with the European catastrophe: the failure of the Enlightenment tradition, the concept of law in the Nuremberg trials, the nature of cruelty and injustice. “The Liberalism of Fear” was published three years before Shklar’s death in 1992, and though it wasn’t one of her major works, the title has become a kind of shorthand for her worldview. As Lilla writes in his introduction, for Shklar, “fear of being in another’s arbitrary power is the ur-human experience that modern liberalism was developed to stave off.” In the essay, she discusses the tools that modern liberal societies use for this purpose. Some of these tools are legal: “Without well-defined procedures, honest judges, opportunities for counsel and for appeals, no one has a chance.” Others are political and economic, such as security for private property: “Nothing gives a person greater social resources than legally guaranteed proprietorship.” [ Read: This is the way a world order ends ] But Shklar is most concerned with the ideas and habits of mind that sustain liberal societies. And it is here that her message for today becomes most urgent. The “perfect liberal,” she writes, “respects other people without condescension, arrogance, humility, or fear. He or she does not insult others with lies or cruelty, both of which mar one’s own character no less than they injure one’s victims.” These aren’t the heroic virtues needed to win wars or found empires; they are minimal requirements for a society free from fear. Until recently, they were expected of anyone who hoped to play a role in American public life, regardless of their political views. Only since Donald Trump got to the White House have Americans realized how much they took for granted the sobriety and politeness of Ronald Reagan or Barack Obama. Trumpism’s assault on liberal democracy isn’t only a matter of laws and policies. From the beginning, it has been about legitimizing cruelty. When Trump mockingly imitated a disabled reporter, or said police officers shouldn’t be “too nice” when putting suspects into police cars, or pardoned an American soldier convicted by a court martial of murdering civilians, he was sending the message that he approves of cruelty, and will support those who commit it. The federal government and the Republican Party resisted that message in his first term; in his second, they have mostly stopped resisting. We are still a long way from the Europe of Shklar’s childhood. America has been a liberal democracy for a long time, and the majority of Americans are not ready to embrace a politics of cruelty. But that prospect feels a lot less theoretical than it did when “The Liberalism of Fear” was written. In the essay, Shklar says that government terror and cruelty weren’t things of the past, but could be seen in “the foreign news in the New York Times.” Now it’s not just the foreign news that reminds us how much we have to be afraid of—and how much we need the values and institutions of liberalism, no matter how unfashionable they’ve become.

items.description: The Ghana Education Service (GES) has transferred the first-term Capitation Grant for the 2026/2027 academic year to District Education Directorates for onward disbursement to basic schools. In a letter dated October 16, 2026, and addressed to all Regional Directors of Education, the Service directed them to ensure that the funds are transferred to the schools on or before Friday, October 30, 2026. The GES said the transfers to district accounts include the Sports and Culture component for district offices, while the corresponding components for regional offices have been transferred to their designated accounts. It urged Regional Directors to ensure the immediate release of the funds to enable heads of basic schools to operate smoothly. The Service also announced that a team from its headquarters would visit the regions for a monitoring exercise in the first week of November 2026. The visits are expected to monitor the disbursement process, making it necessary for regional authorities to ensure that the funds reach the schools before the deadline. The GES expressed confidence in the cooperation of the Regional Directors to facilitate the timely disbursement of the grant and support the smooth operation of basic schools during the first term of the academic year.

items.title: Israeli police arrest 10 over settler attacks on journalist and diplomats in West Bank
items.description: Israeli police say they have arrested 10 suspects in the occupied West Bank after attacks by settlers on an American journalist and European diplomats last week. The unnamed suspects were detained at several locations on suspicion of acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order and illegal construction, according to a statement. Potential evidence and vehicles were also seized. On Friday, masked Israeli settlers beat and severely injured Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine as she covered an olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A day later, diplomats from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church were attacked by masked settlers in nearby Taybeh. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, welcomed the arrests. “A very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat Heidi Levine,” he wrote on X. Settler violence in the West Bank is at an all-time high, according to UN records. However, it has escalated dramatically during this year’s olive harvest, which is essential to Palestinian livelihoods. The Israeli human rights group Yesh Din said on Sunday that it had logged 269 incidents of violence directly related to the olive harvest over the previous 20 days. They included 98 cases of violence and physical assaults against harvesters, as well as crop thefts, and the damaging and burning of olive trees. A BBC team witnessed one of several settler attacks during an olive harvest near Khirbet Abu Falah on Friday, which a local official said injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian-American citizens, as well as Heidi Levine. The veteran photojournalist, who was wearing a flak jacket clearly marked “PRESS” on the front and back, said she was knocked to the ground by a group of settlers, kicked repeatedly, and stripped of her cameras and phone. She suffered four broken vertebrae, a broken rib and lacerations across her body. She required surgery on a finger that was ripped open. In a telephone interview with the BBC’s Today programme from her hospital bed in central Israel on Monday, Levine said it “could have been a lot worse”. “We [journalists] don’t always want to wear flak jackets and helmets – it’s heavy, it can be a pain when other people aren’t wearing them, you feel kind of silly – but we all did and I’m grateful for that.” “I think I would have suffered more serious injuries for sure, especially [to] my head. I tried to keep my face to the ground as much as I possibly could so that protected it… I don’t guess, but I know that I’m actually really, really lucky.” Huckabee called the attack on Levine a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards” and said they should spend years in prison. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump “does not want to see friction or a crisis in the West Bank”. Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he had told Levine that the “despicable behaviour of the perpetrators of this attack does not represent the citizens or the values of the State of Israel”. On Saturday, a delegation of Belgian, French, Polish and Catholic Church envoys visited Taybeh, about 6km (4 miles) to the south of Abu Falah, to watch an olive harvest. Belgium’s Foreign Minister, Maxime Prevot, said a car from its consulate was damaged and that a French mayor, Bernard Baudoux, was assaulted. Video from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy and a man wearing a French tricolour sash slumped beside a vehicle. Reports suggested that stones were thrown. Prevot condemned the attack in the strongest terms and said that Israel, as the occupying power, had to protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. The European Union also demanded “full accountability”. Despite the international condemnation, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office questioned the video evidence and testimony from the incidents in Abu Falah and Taybeh. It described them as “alleged” attacks and said they came amid what it called a “co-ordinated campaign to smear Israel” and West Bank settlers. “I’ve had the president of Israel call me, and he was very, very sweet. He called the attackers thugs, promised to do everything in his power to have them arrested,” Levine told the BBC. “I was just reading another article regarding the prime minister’s response, and it’s shocking to me. It’s a big slap on my face.” She said Netanyahu should have sent a “clear message” telling settlers to end their attacks, “instead of the message that I feel was presented, which is… ‘Keep at it.'” Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem – land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a future state – during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law. At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN’s figures. Twenty-five of those deaths have occurred in the context of settler attacks. Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, the UN says. Israel’s police commissioner, Daniel Levy, said the law applied to everyone in the West Bank, “regardless of identity or affiliation”. However, prosecutions of Israeli settlers accused of attacking Palestinians are rare. Between 2005 and 2025, more than 93% of Israeli police investigations into ideologically-motivated offences committed by Israelis against Palestinians in the West Bank ended without an indictment, according to Yesh Din.

items.title: IHC takes up Imaan, Hadi’s appeals against framing of charges in security breach case
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Monday took up appeals filed by human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, against an anti-terrorism court (ATC) order rejecting their petitions challenging the framing of charges and the inclusion of terrorism-related provisions in the security breach case . The case pertains to the alleged disruption of the security route of an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. A division bench comprising Justice Inaam Ameen Minhas and Justice Shahrukh Arjumand heard the matter on Monday, with Riasat Ali Azad, Zainab Janjua and other lawyers appearing before the court. At the outset, Justice Minhas asked whether the accused had received copies of the relevant documents. Counsel Riasat Ali Azad replied in the negative and said he wanted to examine how the charges had been framed. The counsel argued that the ATC had passed the impugned order without the requisite authority to do so. He said the case had remained pending before the court of Judge Abual Hasanat Mohammad Zulqarnain from March 12, 2025, until recently. Citing the precedent in the Zulfikar Ali Bhutto case, Azad argued that the court in which the challan was submitted was the one authorised to hear the case. He further contended that the accused had not been provided with copies of the relevant documents and that the charges had not been read out in their presence, as they were not physically present in the courtroom at the time. “Legal proceedings cannot move forward in the absence of the accused,” the counsel argued, adding that the charge must be framed in the presence of the accused. He also alleged a violation of a decision of the National Judicial Policy Making Committee. Describing the charge as the foundation of a trial, Azad maintained that any defect in its framing would undermine the legality of the subsequent proceedings. Justice Minhas asked whether the trial was being conducted through a video link. The counsel replied that the proceedings had initially taken place through a video link but had shifted to a jail trial at the most recent hearing. The judge also inquired whose signatures appeared on the charge document. Azad said the document bore his signature, but lacked those of the accused, which, according to him, were legally required. Justice Minhas questioned whether the proceedings could not be conducted through a video link, observing that the accused had been connected through the facility and that their attendance had been recorded when the charges were framed. The counsel, however, insisted that the accused were not present when he signed the documents and requested the court to summon the video recording of the proceedings. He also said the copies had not been delivered to the accused in jail and that an affidavit had been submitted to this effect. Justice Minhas remarked that it appeared the defence had not intended to accept the copies. Azad responded that every application filed by the defence before the ATC had been rejected. He said the defence had requested both the case record and the video recording of the proceedings. The judge subsequently asked where it was stipulated that the accused must be physically produced for the framing of charges. Azad reiterated that the appeals also challenged the inclusion of anti-terrorism provisions in the case and repeatedly urged the high court to halt the trial. “We shall see; we will let you know,” Justice Minhas remarked. Justice Minhas said the court would issue an order and inform the parties accordingly. He concluded that notices had been issued and the court would decide how to proceed once the responses were received. ATC hearing adjourned Meanwhile, ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra conducted the proceedings of the security breach case against Imaan and Hadi at the Adiala jail, where they are incarcerated. Advocate Janjua, representing the accused, withdrew her vakalatnama (authorisation to represent them). Subsequently, the hearing was adjourned until 10am tomorrow (Tuesday). No prosecution witnesses’ statements could be recorded during the hearing. Imaan and Hadi were indicted in the case on Oct 7, when both accused were produced via video link. Hadi had objected to the framing of charges, arguing that he had not yet been provided copies of the case documents and that charges could not be framed before completion of all legal formalities. Advocate Janjua also opposed the indictment, submitting that neither of them had been provided copies of the case record. She further contended that neither of the accused had been allowed to meet their lawyers, and therefore, the requirements for framing charges had not been fulfilled. Imaan and Hadi’s rearrest The lawyer couple has been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the IHC and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association (IHCBA) president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) in a case pertaining to controversial social media posts. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On Sept 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the Supreme Court suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the IHC’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand. The case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio. Imaan and her husband were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added. The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties).

items.title: Dette publique française : la Cour des comptes alerte sur un risque d’«étouffement financier»
items.description: Dans un entretien a La Tribune Dimanche , l'ancienne ministre de l'Action et des Comptes publics tire la sonnette d'alarme sur les finances publiques. La charge de la dette et l'incertitude budgetaire menacent les marges de manœuvre de la France. Amelie de Montchalin avait deja appele fin septembre a un « grand menage » concernant les niches fiscales . « La charge de la dette atteindra deja 90 milliards » Amelie de Montchalin souligne que « la charge de la dette atteindra deja 90 milliards d'euros l'annee prochaine ». Elle precise qu'« une hausse de 100 points de base des taux d'interet […] represente un surcoût annuel de 40 milliards d'euros a un horizon de sept ans. Soit trois fois le budget annuel de la Justice ». 🔵 🇫🇷 « Nous menons la bataille de la vérité » L’ancienne ministre de l’Action et des Comptes publics, @AdeMontchalin, aujourd’hui Première présidente de la @Courdescomptes, alerte sur le risque d’un étouffement financier de la France. « Une hausse de 100 points de base [+1 %] des taux d’intérêt représente un surcoût annuel de 40 milliards d’euros à un horizon de sept ans. Soit quatre fois le budget annuel de la Justice. » Et face aux attaques de responsables politiques : « Les propos de campagne électorale ne nous impressionnent pas. » 📰 L’entretien recueilli par Marie-Pierre Gröndahl et @JeanVicSem est à lire dans La @TribuneDimanche N°159 ⤵ https://t.co/PRU6HSku3p — La Tribune Dimanche (@TribuneDimanche) October 18, 2026 Pour preserver « nos marges de manœuvre et notre souverainete », il est, selon elle, « indispensable » de ramener le deficit public sous la barre des 5 % d'ici 2027. Le projet de budget 2027, actuellement examine a l'Assemblee nationale, vise precisement cet objectif apres 5,4 % attendus en 2026. Mais son adoption reste tres incertaine, faute de majorite claire et alors que l'election presidentielle approche. Sur X, des internautes rappellent le passe proche de la premiere presidente de la Cour des comptes avec l'executif macroniste : « L'alerte vient de la presidente de la Cour des comptes, Amelie de Montchalin. Celle qui etait ministre des Comptes publics jusqu'au debut de l'annee. Pendant des annees, elle a signe les budgets en deficit. Aujourd'hui, elle nous explique que la dette risque de nous etouffer ». 90 milliards d'intérêts l'an prochain. Plus que le budget de l'Éducation nationale hors pensions, juste pour payer le passé. L'alerte vient de la présidente de la Cour des comptes, Amélie de Montchalin. Celle qui était ministre des Comptes publics jusqu'au début de l'année. Pendant des années, elle a signé les budgets en déficit. Aujourd'hui, elle nous explique que la dette risque de nous étouffer. Elle découvre l'incendie après avoir tenu les allumettes. Et en France, on ne renvoie pas le pyromane : on le nomme chef des pompiers. Source : https://t.co/JK48r9hLiq — Le Bon Sens (@AuNomDuBonSens) October 18, 2026 L'examen du texte budgetaire avance difficilement a l'Assemblee avec notamment une mouture aggravee de 8 milliards d'euros debut octobre et encore des milliers d'amendements a traiter.

items.title: GHS to conduct two rounds of HPV vaccination in schools nationwide
items.description: The Ghana Health Service (GHS), in collaboration with the Ghana Education Service (GES) and its partners, is set to conduct two rounds of the Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunisation (PIRI), focusing on Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, in schools nationwide. In a statement signed by the Director-General of the Ghana Health Service, Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, the Service said the exercise would be conducted under the Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunisation (PIRI), in collaboration with the Ghana Education Service (GES), through the School Health Education Programme (SHEP), and its partners. The campaign, scheduled for October and November/December 2026, aims to raise awareness of the routine HPV vaccine, improve vaccination uptake, and ensure that eligible girls are protected against cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases. The first round is scheduled for Monday, October 19 to Friday, October 23, 2026, while the second round will take place from Monday, November 30 to Friday, December 4, 2026. During the exercise, health staff will visit schools across the country to administer the vaccine to eligible girls aged 9 to 14 who have not yet received it. The initiative is intended to strengthen routine immunisation efforts and increase protection against cervical cancer and other diseases associated with HPV infection. The Ghana Health Service has called on school authorities, parents, guardians, teachers and community leaders to support the campaign and cooperate with health teams to ensure its successful implementation. “The Ghana Health Service respectfully calls on all stakeholders, including school authorities, parents, guardians, teachers, and community leaders, to support and cooperate with health teams to ensure the successful implementation of the exercise,” the statement said. The Service reaffirmed its commitment to protecting and promoting the health and well-being of Ghanaians, expressing appreciation for the continued collaboration and support of its partners and stakeholders. “The Ghana Health Service remains committed to protecting and promoting the health and well-being of all Ghanaians. items.title: Diaspora AES résidant au Sénégal: une forte mobilisation pour réaffirmer le soutien aux autorités de l’espace confédéral
items.description: (Dakar, le 19 octobre 2026) La délégation de la Confédération des Etats du Sahel présente dans la capitale sénégalaise dans le cadre des premières négociations formelles avec la CEDEAO, a rencontré les communautés burkinabè, malienne et nigérienne installées au pays de la Teranga, dans la soirée du dimanche 18 octobre 2026. Ce cadre d’échanges directs a permis aux ministres de la Confédération AES, de présenter à leurs compatriotes fortement mobilisés, le sens de leur participation à la réunion avec la CEDEAO, et leur apporter les nouvelles de leurs pays respectifs et de l'espace confédéral de façon plus globale. Et puisque ce cadre se veut surtout un moment pour les ministres en charge de la diaspora d'écouter celle-ci, la parole a été donnée aux communautés des trois pays. Dans leurs interventions, les membres de la diaspora burkinabè malienne et nigérienne, ont exprimé leurs félicitations aux Présidents des Etats de la Confédération AES, pour les victoires engrangées au quotidien sur le terrorisme et pour les avancées sur les plans du développement et de la diplomatie. Ils ont encouragé les dirigeants des trois pays dont ils saluent le leadership et la clairvoyance, à maintenir le cap, dans une démarche de solidarité et en mettant toujours les peuples de l'espace confédéral au cœur de leurs initiatives. En ce qui concerne les doléances et les préoccupations, les communautés de la Confédération AES résidant au Sénégal ont sollicité des démarches de la part de leurs dirigeants, pour une reconnaissance de leurs documents d'identité par les services administratifs et sécuritaires du pays d'accueil. Ils ont également souligné la nécessité de trouver une solution urgente et définitive, aux tracasseries et aux raquettes constatées lors des déplacements routiers dans les trois pays de la Confédération AES, tout en encourageant le développement du transport aérien dans cet espace. La préservation des biens et privilèges ( notamment dans le foncier et l'enseignement) des ressortissants de l’AES après la sortie de la CEDEAO, et la prise en compte de l'expertise de la diaspora dans les politiques publiques, ont également été soulignées par les intervenants. Autre point d'intérêt, les membres de la diaspora AES souhaitent une harmonisation des politiques et réformes des trois pays dans des secteurs clés tels que l'éducation et l'enseignement supérieur, tout en encourageant les autorités de l'AES à accorder une place de choix à la formation professionnelle et aux initiatives d’autonomisation des femmes. En réaction, le Camarade ministre Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE qui a présidé la rencontre et ses homologues, ont remercié leurs compatriotes pour les encouragements et pour la sincérité dans l'expression de leurs préoccupations. Ils les ont rassurés que les préoccupations en lien avec la reconnaissance des documents d'identité et les difficultés d'accès à certains services dans le pays d'accueil, sont déjà prises en compte dans le processus de négociations entamé avec la CEDEAO. Par ailleurs, la question des tracasseries routières est, selon le ministre TRAORE, déjà bien connue des autorités de l'espace confédéral, qui y travaillent dans le cadre de la promotion d'une gouvernance vertueuse dans les trois pays. Il a cependant invité les usagers à jouer leur part de responsabilité, en dénonçant ou en refusant d'être acteurs de ce phénomène car dit-il, « sans la participation des populations ce cycle de raquettes ne saurait pas perdurer ». Les ministres ont félicité les ambassadeurs et les responsables des communautés burkinabè malienne et nigérienne, pour le travail qu'ils abattent en terme de mobilisation de la diaspora AES au Sénégal. Ils ont invité les membres de la diaspora à s'impliquer davantage dans la construction de leur pays, sans forcément attendre que des cadres soient créés pour cela. Un appel a été lancé aux ressortissants maliens, burkinabè et nigériens vivant au Sénégal, à l'unité et au respect des lois et règlements du pays d'accueil, pour ainsi véhiculer une image digne et intègre la Confédération AES. DCRP/MAE L’article Diaspora AES résidant au Sénégal: une forte mobilisation pour réaffirmer le soutien aux autorités de l'espace confédéral est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Weija-Gbawe MP urges urgent repairs to Weija-Mallam highway stretch
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Weija-Gbawe, Jerry Ahmed Shaib, has appealed to the Minister of Roads and Highways, Governs Kwame Agbodza, to order urgent repairs to the Weija Junction-Mallam Overpass stretch of the Kasoa-Cape Coast Highway, citing worsening road conditions and severe traffic congestion. In a letter to the Minister, the MP expressed concern about extensive potholes along the stretch, which he said were causing significant delays and hardship for thousands of commuters who use the road daily. According to Mr Shaib, a journey that would ordinarily take about three minutes from Weija Junction to Mallam can now take more than two hours as motorists struggle to navigate the damaged sections. He said the road serves as a key link between communities in Weija-Gbawe, Kasoa, Winneba, Korle-Bu, Kaneshie, Odorkor, Dansoman and other parts of Accra, making its deteriorating condition a major concern for residents and commercial transport operators. Road condition raises healthcare concerns Mr Shaib also highlighted the potential impact of the congestion on access to healthcare, particularly for people travelling to the Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital and Cocoa Clinic. He warned that delays along the stretch could create additional difficulties for patients seeking medical attention, especially in emergencies where timely access to healthcare is critical. The MP has therefore urged the Minister to direct the Ghana Highway Authority and other relevant agencies to inspect the affected section without delay and undertake immediate repairs to ease congestion and improve traffic flow. MP calls for lasting solution Beyond immediate repairs, Mr Shaib is calling for a long-term intervention to prevent the recurrence of potholes and ensure the road remains motorable. He has proposed proper drainage systems and resurfacing as part of measures to address the underlying problems affecting the stretch. Mr Shaib said his appeal was being made on behalf of residents of the Weija-Gbawe constituency, who continue to bear the effects of the road’s deteriorating condition. He expressed hope that the Minister would treat the matter as urgent and take the necessary steps to reduce commuters’ hardship and improve road safety along the busy highway.

items.title: JAMB warns universities against issuing admission letters
items.description: By Joseph Erunke, Abuja The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board, JAMB, has warned universities in the country against issuing admission letters to candidates seeking admission into their various institutions, insisting that such act was not within their mandate to do so. The registrar, Prof. Segun Aina, stated this when he received a delegation from Veritas University, Bwari, Abuja, which paid him a courtesy visit in his office. According to the registrar, JAMB is the only body statutorily empowered to issue official admission letters to candidates seeking entry into all tertiary institutions in Nigeria, including universities, polytechnics, and colleges of education. Prof. Aina stated that the irony of the situation is that once candidates see a document as emanating from an institution purporting to offer them admission, they believe that it is real. He, therefore, charged universities guilty of this ignoble act to desist, adding that they also have the responsibility of ensuring that those candidates obtain the right documents from the board. Furthermore, he recalled that the Federal Ministry of Education had explicitly mandated that all admissions be conducted through the Central Admissions Processing System (CAPS) and that anything done contrary to that is illegal and invalid. As a consequence, no institution is permitted to substitute its own letters for the official JAMB admission letter issued by the board after a candidate had accepted his admission on CAPS. He added that it is only admission offered through this platform is recognised and would be accepted for the purpose of mobilisation for the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC), among others. The post JAMB warns universities against issuing admission letters appeared first on Vanguard News .

L'état d'urgence, « c'est quand même quelque chose qui est lourd, y compris dans sa mise en place. Donc si c'est nécessaire, évidemment que nous pourrions le faire. A date, la question des couvre-feux, la mise en oeuvre de ces couvre-feux, me paraît davantage adaptée à la situation que nous pouvons connaître. » De son côté, le ministre de l'Intérieur Laurent Nuñez, a annoncé des mesures pour « empêcher d'agir les casseurs pilleurs ». « On va encore renforcer les effectifs de police et de gendarmerie sur le terrain et notamment ce week-end », a expliqué le ministre français, lors d'un point presse aux côtés du Premier ministre alors qu'une nouvelle journée de mobilisation est prévue samedi prochain. « Déjà hier (dimanche) soir, ça a un peu bougé dans Paris, dans certaines agglomérations régionales. Beaucoup de mobilité, beaucoup de réactivité. Tout ça, on va le mettre en place », a-t-il ajouté. items.title: TCDA cracks down on shea companies over pricing and licensing breaches
items.description: The Tree Crops Development Authority (TCDA) has warned companies operating in Ghana’s shea industry of possible prosecution, licence revocation and other sanctions following an enforcement operation that uncovered alleged breaches of pricing, licensing and quality regulations. The operation, conducted on Thursday, October 15, 2026, in Accra and Tamale, involved the Ghana Armed Forces, the Ghana Police Service and National Security. It forms part of efforts to enforce the Tree Crops Development Authority Act, 2019 (Act 1010), and the Tree Crops Development Authority Regulations, 2023 (L.I. 2471). Briefing the media after the exercise, TCDA Chief Executive Officer Dr Andy Osei Okrah said processors, traders, buyers, exporters and aggregators would be held accountable for violating the rules governing the industry. Preliminary findings indicated that some companies were purchasing raw shea nuts below the approved minimum producer price of GH¢9.01 per kilogramme. The price, which took effect on June 1, 2026, is equivalent to GH¢765.63 for an 85-kilogramme bag. Other companies were reportedly buying and selling shea nuts with moisture content exceeding the permitted maximum of 10 per cent. The Authority’s prescribed quality parameters include moisture content of 8 to 10 per cent, free fatty acid levels of 6 to 8 per cent, and impurities ranging from 2 to 4 per cent. These parameters form part of the pricing formula established by the TCDA. Dr Okrah said the Authority would not tolerate disregard for the regulations. “We will not allow companies to disregard the laws governing the shea industry. The approved minimum producer price and quality standards must be respected. Any company found violating these requirements will be held accountable in accordance with the law,” he said. The joint task force inspected companies and buying centres to verify registration and licensing status, supplier records, purchase transactions and compliance with documentation requirements. Officers examined invoices, receipts, purchase registers, payment evidence, purchase orders and contracts to establish whether transactions were properly documented and recorded prices reflected actual payments. The exercise also uncovered alleged irregularities involving unlicensed operations, inadequate supplier information and the failure to produce valid conveyance certificates for consignments in transit. Dr Okrah said accurate documentation and traceability were essential to regulating the industry and monitoring the movement of shea nuts. “It is important for the Authority to know who is buying, who is supplying, where the produce comes from and where it is going. Without proper documentation and traceability, effective regulation becomes difficult,” he said. He added that Regulation 55 of L.I. 2471 provides a framework for strengthening oversight of commodity movements and establishing the origin and destination of produce. Companies identified as non-compliant during the preliminary checks were directed to submit comprehensive lists of their suppliers and aggregators to enable the Authority to verify their registration and licensing status. The TCDA said earlier requests for the information had not produced satisfactory levels of compliance, prompting physical inspections to verify records and address outstanding breaches. Dr Okrah urged the affected companies to regularise their operations, provide accurate records and cooperate with regulatory processes, warning that failure to comply could attract sanctions under the law. The enforcement exercise forms part of the Authority’s efforts to strengthen regulation of Ghana’s shea industry, enforce approved producer prices, improve commodity traceability and promote fair business practices. The TCDA has urged processors, traders, buyers, exporters and aggregators to comply with Act 1010 and L.I. 2471, maintain accurate records and meet their licensing and documentation obligations.

Vive en el Pau Pi, la zona de la playa vieja de Oliva, una de las zonas más afectadas por la dana Adam , donde ha fallecido una mujer este lunes. A las 4.00, recuerda, ha empezado a llover “a lo bestia” y ha comenzado a retirar un poco de agua de su casa. items.title: Kaylia Nemour impressionne aux championnats du monde 2026 de Rotterdam
items.description: Kaylia Nemour est bien partie pour décrocher une nouvelle médaille d’or aux championnats du monde de gymnastique (17-25 octobre). À Rotterdam où se déroule l’édition 2026, la championne algérienne a décroché la première place aux qualifications sur les barres asymétriques. La gymnaste de 19 ans, qui est l’une des stars de cette compétition, a obtenu 14.933 points, ce qui lui permet de prendre la tête du concours général avec 55.999 points. L’Algérienne a obtenu une note de 14.033 points en saut de cheval et 14.133 points sur la poutre. Kaylia Nemour bien partie pour décrocher l’or à Rotterdam Championne olympique aux JO de Paris 2024 et championne du monde à Jakarta en octobre 2025, Kaylia Nemour est bien partie pour enrichir son palmarès, déjà impressionnant, avec d’autres médailles d’or aux championnats du monde de Rotterdam. Reine incontestée des barres asymétriques où elle écrase la concurrence, l’Algérienne s’est beaucoup améliorée sur les autres agrès comme la poutre et le saut de cheval. items.title: Les recettes de voyages du Maroc atteignent un record, portées par les visiteurs français
items.description: Les voyageurs français ont généré 43 milliards de dirhams de recettes pour le Maroc en 2025, confortant la place de la France comme premier marché contributeur aux recettes de voyages du royaume. L’Espagne et l’Italie occupent respectivement les deuxième et troisième positions, selon le rapport annuel de l’Office des changes sur la balance des paiements et la position extérieure globale. La hiérarchie des pays contributeurs est restée relativement stable par rapport à 2024. Les recettes en provenance de France ont progressé de 16,5 %, passant de 36,9 milliards de dirhams à 43 milliards. Celles générées par les voyageurs espagnols ont atteint 20,5 milliards de dirhams, en hausse de 17,9 %. L’Italie a enregistré la progression la plus marquée parmi ces trois pays, avec une augmentation de 26,8 %, portant ses recettes à 10,6 milliards de dirhams. Ces chiffres portent sur les recettes de voyages, une catégorie statistique qui englobe les dépenses des visiteurs étrangers, quels que soient les motifs de leur déplacement, notamment les loisirs, le travail, les études ou les soins médicaux. Elle se distingue des seules recettes touristiques, limitées aux dépenses des visiteurs venus pour les loisirs et les vacances. Un excédent de 105,4 milliards de dirhams À l’échelle nationale, les recettes de voyages ont atteint un niveau record de 138,6 milliards de dirhams à la fin de 2025, contre 114,5 milliards un an auparavant, soit une progression de 21 %. Principale composante des échanges de services dans la balance des paiements, ce poste a ainsi contribué à renforcer les recettes extérieures du royaume. Dans le même temps, les dépenses de voyages à l’étranger ont augmenté de 13,2 %, passant de 29,4 milliards de dirhams en 2024 à 33,2 milliards en 2025, soit une hausse de 3,8 milliards. L’écart entre les recettes et les dépenses a permis de dégager un excédent de 105,4 milliards de dirhams, en progression de 23,8 % par rapport aux 85,1 milliards enregistrés en 2024. Les voyages à titre personnel constituent la principale composante de ce poste, aussi bien du côté des recettes que des dépenses. En 2025, leur solde excédentaire a augmenté de 23,7 %, passant de 81,3 milliards à 100,5 milliards de dirhams. Cette évolution s’explique par une hausse des recettes de 23 milliards de dirhams, supérieure à l’augmentation des dépenses, qui s’est limitée à 3,8 milliards. Les voyages à titre professionnel ont également affiché un solde positif en hausse. Celui-ci s’est établi à 4,8 milliards de dirhams en 2025, contre 3,8 milliards en 2024, soit une progression de 26,3 %, équivalant à un milliard de dirhams supplémentaire. Le déficit des services de transport se creuse À l’inverse, les services de transport, deuxième composante des échanges de services après les voyages en termes de recettes et de dépenses, ont vu leur déficit se creuser de 10,8 % en 2025. Leurs recettes ont progressé de 5,6 %, pour atteindre 46,6 milliards de dirhams, contre 44,2 milliards en 2024. Cette augmentation est toutefois restée inférieure à celle des dépenses, qui ont crû de 6,8 %, passant de 58,1 milliards à 62,1 milliards de dirhams sur la même période. La progression des recettes s’explique principalement par la hausse des revenus du transport maritime et aérien. Les recettes du transport maritime ont augmenté de 6,1 %, soit 1,3 milliard de dirhams supplémentaire, pour atteindre 22,4 milliards en 2025, contre 21,1 milliards en 2024. Celles du transport aérien ont progressé de 5,5 %, soit 1,1 milliard de dirhams, pour s’établir à 21 milliards, contre 19,9 milliards un an auparavant. Les recettes des autres modes de transport ont, pour leur part, augmenté de 2,4 %. Du côté des dépenses, la hausse est notamment liée au transport aérien, dont la facture a progressé de 11,1 %, soit 1,4 milliard de dirhams, pour atteindre 13,8 milliards en 2025, contre 12,4 milliards en 2024. Les dépenses de transport maritime ont également augmenté de 6 %, soit 2,5 milliards de dirhams supplémentaires, pour s’établir à 43,3 milliards, contre 40,8 milliards l’année précédente. Enfin, les dépenses consacrées aux autres modes de transport ont progressé de 3,2 %. The post Les recettes de voyages du Maroc atteignent un record, portées par les visiteurs français appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: IA et création littéraire : le monde de l’édition en quête de garde-fous
items.description: Alors que la déferlante IA continue à progresser et s’imposer en révolution incontournable bouleversant les différents aspects de notre quotidien, la polémique autour de son utilisation inquiète en France particulièrement le monde de l’édition qui s’interroge sur les moyens de préserver la création littéraire « humaine ». Entre appels à une régulation et plus de transparence, voire même une labellisation « 100 % humain », depuis la récente disqualification, sous soupçons de recours à l'Intelligence artificielle et d'accusations de plagiat, d’un auteur du prestigieux Prix Goncourt 2026, des voix s’élèvent pour dénoncer une concurrence « déloyale » qui menace l'authenticité créative des œuvres littéraires. Dans la foulée d’une polémique à dimension internationale, l’académie Goncourt avait pris, le 25 septembre, une décision radicale, celle d’une suppression pure et simple du roman « C'était ça ou mourir » de l’écrivain canado-haïtien Thélyson Orélien (Éditions Grasset), de la première sélection de son prix éponyme qui sera décerné le 3 novembre. Pour justifier cette décision, l’académie française avait affirmé alors tenir compte « des plagiats dont son auteur s'est rendu coupable au fil du temps et qui viennent d'être révélés, ainsi que du résultat convergent de plusieurs analyses de chercheurs et journalistes dignes de foi mettant en évidence le fait que C'était ça ou mourir (…) est selon toute vraisemblance très largement le produit d'une Intelligence artificielle ». « Ce choix est dicté par la volonté de préserver l'intégrité du prix Goncourt, celle de l'Académie, dont le rôle central consiste à promouvoir et couronner la littérature écrite par des femmes et des hommes », avait-elle expliqué dans un communiqué. Pour l’institution, il s'agit d' « envoyer un message clair – et notamment aux participants du Prix Goncourt des Lycéens, du Goncourt des Détenus et ceux des plus de cinquante Choix Goncourt de l'Étranger : un message qui affirme que nous ne cautionnons ni n'adoubons d'une façon ou d'une autre la création de textes générés avec l’aide de l’IA ». Même si l’écrivain disqualifié de la liste des « goncourables » (mais demeure en tête des ventes dans l’Hexagone), maintient ne pas avoir eu recours à cette technologie pour écrire son roman, tout en présentant « ses excuses » pour des erreurs de plagiat commises dans le passé, l’affaire Orélien relance le débat sur l’avenir de la création humaine à l’ère de l’IA dans la production littéraire. La romancière marocaine Zineb Mekouar, lauréate de plusieurs prix littéraires en France, est optimiste à cet égard, partant de la conviction que la réponse tient d’abord à la rencontre entre deux sensibilités humaines. « Pour moi, la littérature, c’est un dialogue d’âme à âme. C’est un dialogue différé d’âme à âme », confie-t-elle dans une déclaration à la MAP. L’écrivaine distingue la capacité d’une machine à produire un récit de ce que motive, à ses yeux, l’expérience littéraire. Un livre, décrypte-t-elle, porte une histoire personnelle, des émotions, des souvenirs et une vision du monde, même lorsqu’il relève de la fiction. « Ce qui m’intéresse dans l’expérience même de lecture et d’écriture, c’est cette rencontre avec un autre humain », souligne-t-elle. Pragmatique, l’autrice considère néanmoins qu’à l’ère de l’IA, la priorité est, d’abord, d’établir des règles claires. « Le tout, c’est d’être transparent, en fait, avec le lecteur », explique celle qui défend un système de signalement précisant les conditions de production d’un livre (« écrit sans IA », « 100% humain », « écrit à l'aide de l'IA pour des recherches », …) « Je pense vraiment que, comme beaucoup de bouleversements technologiques, on va apprendre à vivre avec l’IA, mais la mise en place d’un cadre éthique est indispensable », insiste-t-elle, avant de conclure : « Il faut pouvoir choisir et en connaissance de cause ». Au-delà du débat esthétique, l’essor de l’IA générative soulève aussi des craintes d’ordre économique et professionnel, selon les spécialistes du secteur de l’édition. Plusieurs d’entre eux mettent en garde notamment contre une éventuelle « concurrence déloyale », favorisée par un système capable de produire rapidement des centaines de pages à partir d’instructions, à même de bouleverser les conditions de travail des auteurs, alors qu’un roman humain résulte souvent de plusieurs années d’élaboration. D’aucuns soulignent, en revanche, l’impératif de distinguer l’IA utilisée pour documenter un sujet, corriger un texte ou organiser des recherches de celle qui génère des passages entiers, voire un manuscrit complet. The post IA et création littéraire : le monde de l’édition en quête de garde-fous appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Photos: COAS visits Rwanda genocide memorial, urges national unity
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi The Chief of Army Staff (COAS), Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has highlighted the importance of national unity, religious tolerance and peaceful coexistence following his visit to the Kigali Genocide Memorial in Rwanda. Shaibu, who visited the memorial on Monday as part of his ongoing working visit to Rwanda, said the country’s tragic history offered important lessons on the devastating consequences of ethnic hatred, divisive rhetoric and violent extremism. The Kigali Genocide Memorial houses the remains of approximately 250,000 victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, serving as a solemn reminder of the dangers of unchecked hatred, political manipulation and national disunity. A statement by the Acting Director of Army Public Relations, Colonel Appolonia Anele, said the visit underscored the need for Nigerians to rise above ethnic, religious and political differences in the collective pursuit of national peace and stability. The statement noted that Rwanda’s experience reinforced the importance of rejecting hate speech, embracing tolerance and promoting patriotism and collective responsibility among citizens. It added that the visit highlighted the critical roles of responsible leadership, early conflict prevention and sustained civil-military cooperation in preventing violent conflicts and strengthening national cohesion. The Nigerian Army chief’s visit comes amid continuing security challenges in Nigeria, reinforcing the importance of unity and collaboration in addressing threats to national peace and stability. The Army reiterated that national unity remains fundamental to achieving enduring peace, security and sustainable development. items.title: Niakhène : Plus de 1 000 personnes enrôlées à la Couverture sanitaire universelle
items.description: Plus de 1 000 personnes vulnérables ont été enrôlées gratuitement à la Couverture sanitaire universelle (CSU) dans la commune de Niakhène, département de Tivaouane, grâce à une initiative du Dr Abdou Lahat Guèye, responsable du parti Pastef dans la localité. Au total, ce sont plus de 650 personnes, dont des femmes, des personnes du troisième âge, des Serigne Daara et des talibés, qui ont reçu sur place leur carte de CSU, lors d'une cérémonie de signature de convention organisée à Niakhène, ce dimanche 18 octobre, au poste de santé de la zone, entre Mme Anta Mbaye Diop, présidente de la mutuelle départementale de Tivaouane, et le Dr Abdou Lahad Guèye, responsable de Pastef, pour un an. La veille, 350 cartes avaient déjà été produites et remises aux bénéficiaires dans le village de Khawlou, portant le total à 1 000 personnes bénéficiaires. Pour permettre à ces populations vulnérables de bénéficier d'une prise en charge à 80 % dans les structures de santé publiques, le Dr Guèye a signé une convention avec la mutuelle de santé départementale de Tivaouane. Selon Anta Mbaye Diop, présidente du conseil d'administration de la mutuelle, « de telles initiatives privées sont salutaires et permettent aux populations du monde rural, souvent dépourvues de moyens, de pouvoir se soigner et, par ricochet, d'accompagner la politique de l'État dans le domaine de la santé », a-t-elle magnifié. Pour faciliter l'opération, l'Agence régionale de la Couverture maladie de Thiès a mobilisé une équipe technique pour produire et remettre les cartes sur place, tandis que le personnel de Tivaouane s'est chargé de la collecte des données. Le Dr Guèye s'est réjoui de la forte mobilisation. Face à l'engouement, il a décidé d'augmenter le nombre de bénéficiaires initialement prévu. L'année dernière déjà, le responsable de Pastef avait offert 300 cartes aux populations. « Pastef est dans la politique de développement et non dans des bavardages inutiles. Le parti et une bonne partie des populations ont compris que le développement de ce pays se fera par nous-mêmes », a rappelé le pharmacien. « Pour porter le développement, il faut une population saine, d'où ce don de 1 000 cartes », a-t-il ajouté. Un avis partagé par Bassirou Sall, président du collectif des chefs de villages de l'arrondissement de Niakhène et secrétaire général de l'antenne CMU : « Beaucoup de gens tombent malades et ne se rendent pas dans les structures de santé faute de moyens financiers. » Cet enrôlement est d'une importance capitale, d’autant plus que la santé est devenue coûteuse, a-t-il estimé. Même son de cloche chez Serigne Mor Talla Dieng, coordonnateur des 60 daara de Niakhène, et Sokhna Ndèye Dieng, femme leader engagée pour le développement de Niakhène. Le coordonnateur communal de Pastef à Niakhène, Pape Birame Gaye, s'est, quant à lui, réjoui des actions de solidarité du Dr Guèye qui, selon lui, honorent le parti dans la commune. Ibrahima NDIAYE (Correspondant)

items.title: Affaire Lionel Bilgo : Le dossier renvoyé au 16 novembre dans l’attente d’une décision de la Cour d’appel
items.description: Le procès de l’ancien ministre de l’Éducation nationale, Lionel Bilgo, et de Vincent de Paul Kaboré, respectivement gérant et directeur exécutif de la Société immobilière Traoré et Frères (SITRAF), a été renvoyé au 16 novembre 2026 par le Pôle économique et financier (ECOFI) du Tribunal de grande instance (TGI) de Bobo-Dioulasso. La décision a été prise à l’audience du lundi 19 octobre 2026, dans l’attente de la décision de la Cour d’appel sur le dessaisissement de la chambre correctionnelle au profit du Pôle économique et financier (ECOFI). À l’ouverture du dossier, le ministère public a sollicité un renvoi au 2 novembre 2026, le temps que la Cour d’appel se prononce sur la juridiction compétente pour connaître de l’affaire. Les avocats de la défense ne se sont pas opposés à cette demande. Ils ont toutefois souhaité que le dossier soit renvoyé à une date plus éloignée ou inscrit au rôle général, afin de s’assurer que la décision de la Cour d’appel soit rendue avant la prochaine audience. À l’issue des échanges, le tribunal a décidé de renvoyer l’affaire au 16 novembre prochain, toujours dans l’attente de la décision de la juridiction d’appel. Pour rappel, Lionel Bilgo et Vincent de Paul Kaboré ont bénéficié d’une liberté provisoire sous caution, le mercredi 14 octobre 2026, à la suite d’une décision favorable de la Cour d’appel. Chacun des deux prévenus a versé une caution de 20 millions de francs CFA pour bénéficier de cette mesure. Le dossier porte notamment sur des faits présumés liés à l’exercice d’activités foncières et à la promotion immobilière, dont la vente de places nues sans autorisation préalable. Le volet relatif au blanchiment de capitaux avait conduit la chambre correctionnelle du TGI de Bobo-Dioulasso à se dessaisir du dossier au profit du Pôle ECOFI. La défense ayant contesté cette décision, la Cour d’appel doit se prononcer sur le dessaisissement. L’examen de l’affaire au fond reste ainsi suspendu à l’évolution de cette procédure. Noufou NEBIE
